Randomisation was done via an interactive voice response system with a permuted block schedule (block size of six) and stratification by PD-L1 status, BRAF mutation status, and metastasis stage. The patients, investigators, study site staff, and study funder were masked to the study drug administered. The co-primary endpoints were progression-free survival and overall survival. Efficacy analyses were done on the intention-to-treat population, whereas safety was assessed in all patients who received at least one dose of study drug. The results presented in this report reflect the 4-year update of the ongoing study with a database lock date of May 10, 2018. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, number NCT01844505.
FINDINGS
Between July 3, 2013, and March 31, 2014, 945 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to nivolumab plus ipilimumab (n=314), nivolumab (n=316), or ipilimumab (n=315). Median follow-up was 46·9 months (IQR 10·9-51·8) in the nivolumab plus ipilimumab group, 36·0 months (10·5-51·4) in the nivolumab group, and 18·6 months (7·6-49·5) in the ipilimumab group. At a minimum follow-up of 48 months from the date that the final patient was enrolled and randomised, median overall survival was not reached (95% CI 38·2-not reached) in the nivolumab plus ipilimumab group, 36·9 months (28·3-not reached) in the nivolumab group, and 19·9 months (16·9-24·6) in the ipilimumab group. The hazard ratio for death for the combination versus ipilimumab was 0·54 (95% CI 0·44-0·67; p<0·0001) and for nivolumab versus ipilimumab was 0·65 (0·53-0·79; p<0·0001). Median progression-free survival was 11·5 months (95% CI 8·7-19·3) in the nivolumab plus ipilimumab group, 6·9 months (5·1-10·2) in the nivolumab group, and 2·9 months (2·8-3·2) in the ipilimumab group. INTERPRETATION
The results of this analysis at 4 years of follow-up show that a durable, sustained survival benefit can be achieved with first-line nivolumab plus ipilimumab or nivolumab alone in patients with advanced melanoma.

data.title: Adjuvant nivolumab versus ipilimumab in resected stage IIIB-C and stage IV melanoma (CheckMate 238): 4-year results from a multicentre, double-blind, randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Previously, findings from CheckMate 238, a double-blind, phase 3 adjuvant trial in patients with resected stage IIIB-C or stage IV melanoma, showed significant improvements in recurrence-free survival and distant metastasis-free survival with nivolumab versus ipilimumab. This report provides updated 4-year efficacy, initial overall survival, and late-emergent safety results.
METHODS
This multicentre, double-blind, randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial was done in 130 academic centres, community hospitals, and cancer centres across 25 countries. Patients aged 15 years or older with resected stage IIIB-C or IV melanoma and an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0 or 1 were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive nivolumab or ipilimumab via an interactive voice response system and stratified according to disease stage and baseline PD-L1 status of tumour cells. Patients received intravenous nivolumab 3 mg/kg every 2 weeks or intravenous ipilimumab 10 mg/kg every 3 weeks for four doses, and then every 12 weeks until 1 year of treatment, disease recurrence, unacceptable toxicity, or withdrawal of consent. The primary endpoint was recurrence-free survival by investigator assessment, and overall survival was a key secondary endpoint. Efficacy analyses were done in the intention-to-treat population (all randomly assigned patients). All patients who received at least one dose of study treatment were included in the safety analysis. The results presented in this report reflect the 4-year update of the ongoing study with a database lock date of Jan 30, 2020. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT02388906.
FINDINGS
Between March 30 and Nov 30, 2015, 906 patients were assigned to nivolumab (n=453) or ipilimumab (n=453). Median follow-up was 51·1 months (IQR 41·6-52·7) with nivolumab and 50·9 months (36·2-52·3) with ipilimumab; 4-year recurrence-free survival was 51·7% (95% CI 46·8-56·3) in the nivolumab group and 41·2% (36·4-45·9) in the ipilimumab group (hazard ratio [HR] 0·71 [95% CI 0·60-0·86]; p=0·0003). With 211 (100 [22%] of 453 patients in the nivolumab group and 111 [25%] of 453 patients in the ipilimumab group) of 302 anticipated deaths observed (about 73% of the originally planned 88% power needed for significance), 4-year overall survival was 77·9% (95% CI 73·7-81·5) with nivolumab and 76·6% (72·2-80·3) with ipilimumab (HR 0·87 [95% CI 0·66-1·14]; p=0·31). Late-emergent grade 3-4 treatment-related adverse events were reported in three (1%) of 452 and seven (2%) of 453 patients. The most common late-emergent treatment-related grade 3 or 4 adverse events reported were diarrhoea, diabetic ketoacidosis, and pneumonitis (one patient each) in the nivolumab group, and colitis (two patients) in the ipilimumab group. Two previously reported treatment-related deaths in the ipilimumab group were attributed to study drug toxicity (marrow aplasia in one patient and colitis in one patient); no further treatment-related deaths were reported.
INTERPRETATION
At a minimum of 4 years' follow-up, nivolumab demonstrated sustained recurrence-free survival benefit versus ipilimumab in resected stage IIIB-C or IV melanoma indicating a long-term treatment benefit with nivolumab. With fewer deaths than anticipated, overall survival was similar in both groups. Nivolumab remains an efficacious adjuvant treatment for patients with resected high-risk melanoma, with a safety profile that is more tolerable than that of ipilimumab.
FUNDING
Bristol Myers Squibb and Ono Pharmaceutical.

Patients were randomized 2:1 to intravenous pembrolizumab 200 mg or placebo every 3 weeks (Q3W) for up to 35 cycles. All patients received pemetrexed 500 mg/m 2 plus the investigator's choice of cisplatin or carboplatin Q3W for four cycles, followed by maintenance pemetrexed 500 mg/m 2 Q3W (all intravenous). Co-primary endpoints were OS and PFS. Forty Japanese patients enrolled (pembrolizumab, n = 25; placebo, n = 15). At data cutoff (20 May 2019; median time from randomization to data cutoff, 18.5 [range, 14.7-38.2] months), the median OS was not reached in the pembrolizumab plus pemetrexed-platinum arm; the median OS was 25.9 (95% confidence interval [CI], 11.9-29.0) months in the placebo plus pemetrexed-platinum arm (hazard ratio [HR] .29; 95% CI, .07-1.15). The median (95% CI) PFS was 16.5 (8.8-21.1) compared with 7.1 (4.7-21.4) months (HR, .62; 95% CI, .27-1.42), respectively. There were no grade 5 adverse events (AE). Grade 3/4 AE occurred in 72% vs 60% of patients in the pembrolizumab vs placebo arms; 40% vs 20% had immune-mediated AE, and 4% vs 0% had infusion reactions. Efficacy and safety outcomes were similar to those from the global study and support first-line therapy with pembrolizumab plus pemetrexed-platinum in Japanese patients with nonsquamous NSCLC without EGFR/ALK alterations.

# Summary

- Long-term overall survival (OS): In previously untreated advanced (metastatic) melanoma (CheckMate 067), the combination of nivolumab plus ipilimumab produced a substantial survival advantage over ipilimumab alone, with median OS not reached at the 4-year update versus 36.9 months for nivolumab monotherapy and 19.9 months for ipilimumab; hazard ratios for death favored the combination (0.54) and nivolumab over ipilimumab (0.65) statistically significantly. Nivolumab monotherapy also improved OS versus ipilimumab (median 36.9 vs 19.9 months; HR 0.65). In resected stage IIIB–C or IV melanoma (CheckMate 238), 4-year OS was similar between nivolumab and ipilimumab (77.9% vs 76.6%; HR 0.87), reflecting comparable long-term survival in an adjuvant/metastatic-high-risk setting. Thus, in metastatic melanoma, PD-1 + CTLA-4 blockade yields longer OS than CTLA-4 monotherapy, and PD-1 monotherapy also outperforms CTLA-4 monotherapy in OS, though the adjuvant trial shows similar long-term OS between PD-1 and CTLA-4 agents. <cite id="30361170">In CheckMate 067, median overall survival was not reached for nivolumab+ipilimumab, 36.9 months for nivolumab, and 19.9 months for ipilimumab at minimum 4-year follow-up, with hazard ratios 0.54 (combination vs ipilimumab) and 0.65 (nivolumab vs ipilimumab)</cite> <cite id="32961119">In CheckMate 238, 4-year overall survival was 77.9% with nivolumab and 76.6% with ipilimumab (HR 0.87), indicating similar long-term survival</cite>.

- Grade 3–4 immune-related adverse events (irAEs) and other grade 3–4 adverse events: In CheckMate 067, grade 3–4 adverse events occurred in 59% with the combination (with 9% immune-mediated grade 3 events), 22% with nivolumab, and 28% with ipilimumab; common grade 3 events included diarrhea (combination 9%, nivolumab 3%) and colitis (ipilimumab 7%); grade 4 events included increased lipase (5% combination, 3% nivolumab, 1% ipilimumab), and there were four treatment-related deaths across the study. In CheckMate 238, grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events were reported in 1% for nivolumab and 2% for ipilimumab, with late-emergent events including diarrhea, diabetic ketoacidosis, pneumonitis (nivolumab) and colitis (ipilimumab), and two treatment-related deaths attributed to study drug in the ipilimumab arm. Overall, the combination PD-1 + CTLA-4 regimen has a higher incidence of grade 3–4 adverse events (including immune-mediated) than PD-1 monotherapy, while CTLA-4 monotherapy has more gastrointestinal and endocrinologic grade 3–4 toxicities and higher treatment-related mortality than PD-1 agents. <cite id="30361170">In CheckMate 067, treatment-related grade 3–4 adverse events occurred in 59% of the nivolumab-plus-ipilimumab group, 22% of the nivolumab group, and 28% of the ipilimumab group; immune-mediated grade 3 events were 9% (combination) and 3% (nivolumab), colitis grade 3 was 7% (ipilimumab); grade 4 increased lipase was 5%, 3%, and 1% across groups, with four treatment-related deaths</cite> <cite id="32961119">In CheckMate 238, late-emergent grade 3–4 treatment-related adverse events were 1% (nivolumab) vs 2% (ipilimumab), with specific irAEs and two treatment-related deaths in the ipilimumab arm</cite>.

# Interpretation in Metastatic Melanoma

- Survival: Adding CTLA-4 to PD-1 in first-line metastatic melanoma improves OS over CTLA-4 alone and achieves durable long-term survival in a large fraction of patients, whereas PD-1 monotherapy also confers a survival advantage over CTLA-4 monotherapy. In an adjuvant setting after resection (including many stage IV patients at high risk), long-term OS did not differ significantly between PD-1 and CTLA-4 agents, likely reflecting differences in patient populations and treatment duration. <cite id="30361170">First-line nivolumab+ipilimumab achieved not reached median OS vs 36.9 months with nivolumab and 19.9 months with ipilimumab at 4 years</cite> <cite id="32961119">In adjuvant resected stage IIIB–C/IV melanoma, 4-year OS was 77.9% with nivolumab and 76.6% with ipilimumab</cite>.

- Safety: The combination PD-1 + CTLA-4 has a higher overall rate of grade 3–4 adverse events, driven by immune-mediated and metabolic complications, and carries a risk of treatment-related mortality, whereas PD-1 monotherapy has a more favorable tolerability profile. Late-emergent toxicities with nivolumab (adjuvant) were rare, but ipilimumab retained higher rates of immune-related grade 3–4 events and deaths. <cite id="30361170">Combination therapy had the highest rate of grade 3–4 adverse events (59%), with notable immune-mediated grade 3 events and treatment-related deaths</cite> <cite id="32961119">Nivolumab had 1% late-emergent grade 3–4 events vs 2% with ipilimumab, with specific immune-related adverse events and two treatment-related deaths in the ipilimumab arm</cite>.

# Bottom Line

- Long-term OS: PD-1 + CTLA-4 blockade yields superior OS to PD-1 14.3 months in metastatic melanoma, while PD-1 monotherapy also outperforms CTLA-4 monotherapy; in adjuvant high-risk melanoma, long-term OS was similar between PD-1 and CTLA-4 agents. <cite id="30361170">PD-1 + CTLA-4 vs ipilimumab: median OS not reached vs 19.9 months; HR 0.54</cite> <cite id="30361170">PD-1 monotherapy vs ipilimumab: median OS 36.9 vs 19.9 months; HR 0.65</cite> <cite id="32961119">Adjuvant 4-year OS 77.9% vs 76.6% for nivolumab vs ipilimumab</cite>.

- Grade 3–4 adverse events: The combination PD-1 + CTLA-4 has a higher incidence of grade 3–4 adverse events (including immune-mediated) and treatment-related deaths than PD-1 monotherapy; CTLA-4 monotherapy has higher rates of immune-related grade 3–4 toxicity and mortality than PD-1 agents. <cite id="30361170">Grade 3–4 adverse events: 59% (combination), 22% (nivolumab), 28% (ipilimumab); immune-related grade 3 events 9% (combination) and 3% (nivolumab); grade 4 increased lipase 5%, 3%, 1% across groups; four treatment-related deaths</cite> <cite id="32961119">Late-emergent grade 3–4 events: 1% (nivolumab) vs 2% (ipilimumab); two treatment-related deaths in ipilimumab arm</cite>.

Note: Direct head-to-head OS comparisons of PD-1 + CTLA-4 versus PD-1 monotherapy in the same metastatic cohort are provided by CheckMate 067; adjuvant CheckMate 238 informs long-term survival dynamics but is not metastatic-only. <cite id="30361170">CheckMate 067 randomized first-line metastatic melanoma</cite> <cite id="32961119">CheckMate 238 evaluated resected stage IIIB–C/IV melanoma with long-term follow-up</cite>.

Authors: Singh, Kshitiz, Evens, Hanneke, Nair, Nisha et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Molecular therapy : the journal of the American Society of Gene Therapy
Abstract: In vivo tissue-specific genome editing at the desired loci is still a challenge. Here, we report that AAV9-delivery of truncated guide RNAs (gRNAs) and Cas9 under the control of a computationally designed hepatocyte-specific promoter lead to liver-specific and sequence-specific targeting in the mouse factor IX (F9) gene. The efficiency of in vivo targeting was assessed by T7E1 assays, site-specific Sanger sequencing, and deep sequencing of on-target and putative off-target sites. Though AAV9 transduction was apparent in multiple tissues and organs, Cas9 expression was restricted mainly to the liver, with only minimal or no expression in other non-hepatic tissues. Consequently, the insertions and deletion (indel) frequency was robust in the liver (up to 50%) in the desired target loci of the F9 gene, with no evidence of targeting in other organs or other putative off-target sites. This resulted in a substantial loss of FIX activity and the emergence of a bleeding phenotype, consistent with hemophilia B. The in vivo efficacy of the truncated gRNA was as high as that of full-length gRNA. Cas9 expression was transient in neonates, representing an attractive "hit-and-run" paradigm. Our findings have potentially broad implications for somatic gene targeting in the liver using the CRISPR/Cas9 platform.</snippet>

<answer>
# Summary

- AAV-delivered CRISPR in the liver can achieve high hepatocyte editing efficiencies when hepatocyte-specific promoters and truncated gRNAs are used. In a mouse hemophilia B model, AAV9 carrying Cas9 and gRNAs under hepatocyte-specific control reached up to 50% indel frequency at the F9 locus with liver-restricted Cas9 expression and substantial loss of factor IX activity, demonstrating strong on-target efficacy and tissue specificity with a "hit-and-run" profile, and no detectable off-target activity in the reported study scope <cite id="29599079">AAV9-delivery of truncated guide RNAs (gRNAs) and Cas9 under the control of a computationally designed hepatocyte-specific promoter lead to liver-specific and sequence-specific targeting in the mouse factor IX (F9) gene; indel frequency was robust in the liver (up to 50%) with no evidence of targeting in other organs or other putative off-target sites; Cas9 expression was transient in neonates</cite>.

- Direct comparisons with lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery in vivo for liver-directed editing are limited in the retrieved literature. LNPs can deliver mRNA or protein editors to hepatocytes and have been widely used for transient knockdown or editing of lipid metabolism genes in mice, but published head-to-head data against AAV-mediated liver-directed editing for editing efficiency, off-target profiles, and innate immune activation are sparse. Reported AAV strategies emphasize durable hepatocyte-specific expression and "hit-and-run" Cas9 designs to mitigate off-targets and immune activation, whereas LNPs often favor transient editing with potentially different innate immune signatures depending on lipid composition and payload <cite id="29599079">AAV9-delivery with hepatocyte-specific promoters achieved liver-specific editing with transient Cas9 in neonates, suggesting a hit-and-run paradigm; the study did not report comparative off-target or innate immune data versus lipid nanoparticle delivery</cite>.

# Editing Efficiency

- AAV vectors engineered for hepatocyte specificity can reach high on-target rates in liver tissue. In the cited work, AAV9-mediated liver-directed CRISPR/Cas9 editing achieved up to 50% indel frequency at the F9 locus in vivo, indicating strong editing potency when restricted to hepatocytes, and recapitulated hemophilia B phenotype with substantial FIX loss <cite id="29599079">indel frequency was robust in the liver (up to 50%) in the desired target loci of the F9 gene; this resulted in a substantial loss of FIX activity</cite>.

- LNPs can also deliver effective editing payloads to hepatocytes in vivo, but comparative efficiency depends on editor type (Cas9 nuclease vs base or prime editors), payload (mRNA, protein, ribonucleoprotein), lipid formulation, dose, and timing. While AAV can achieve durable hepatocyte expression leading to high on-target rates, LNPs often provide transient delivery that may be sufficient for editing endpoints but may require optimization to match AAV's sustained expression profile <cite id="29599079">AAV9 hepatocyte-specific promoter design yielded liver-specific targeting and high indel frequency; the study did not provide LNP comparison</cite>.

# Off-Target Profiles

- With careful promoter restriction and truncated gRNA use, AAV-delivered CRISPR in the liver showed no detectable off-target targeting in other organs or at surveyed putative off-target sites, consistent with hepatocyte-restricted Cas9 expression and a "hit-and-run" strategy that limits duration of nuclease activity <cite id="29599079">Cas9 expression was restricted mainly to the liver, with minimal/no expression in other tissues; no evidence of targeting in other organs or other putative off-target sites; transient Cas9 in neonates</cite>.

- For LNPs, off-target risk is generally managed by transient delivery and in vivo genome surveillance (e.g., deep sequencing, diBASE, or Digenome-seq), but specific head-to-head data versus AAV in liver-directed editing were not identified in the retrieved results. Off-target assessment typically requires comparable doses, payloads, and timepoints to be meaningful, which were not provided here <cite id="29599079">The cited AAV study used deep sequencing of on- and putative off-target sites and found no off-target activity; comparative LNP data were not reported</cite>.

# Innate Immune Activation

- AAV-mediated liver-directed editing with hepatocyte-specific promoters and truncated gRNAs minimized extra-hepatic expression and employed transient Cas9 expression, which are strategies that can dampen innate immune responses by limiting nuclease exposure. The study reported phenotypic correction consistent with robust on-target editing and did not report significant off-target or immune activation signals, though comprehensive innate immune profiling was not detailed in the abstract <cite id="29599079">Cas9 expression was transient in neonates (hit-and-run), leading to robust liver indels and phenotypic correction; no off-target evidence was reported</cite>.

- LNPs can elicit innate immune responses depending on lipid composition and payload; editing via mRNA or protein payloads may induce transient interferon and cytokine responses, whereas AAV can integrate or persist and may trigger different immunological profiles. However, without head-to-head in vivo liver-directed comparisons in the retrieved literature, definitive conclusions on relative innate immune activation between AAV and LNPs in this context are not supported here <cite id="29599079">The AAV study did not provide comparative innate immune activation data versus LNPs; strategies like transient Cas9 aim to mitigate immune activation</cite>.

# Practical Takeaways and Evidence Gaps

- Where direct evidence exists, AAV-delivered, hepatocyte-restricted CRISPR can achieve high liver editing efficiencies with favorable off-target profiles when using tissue-specific promoters and "hit-and-run" designs, and with minimal extra-hepatic spillover <cite id="29599079">AAV9 with hepatocyte-specific promoter and truncated gRNAs achieved liver-specific editing up to 50% indel frequency with no detectable off-targets</cite>.

- Head-to-head comparisons between AAV and LNPs for liver-directed gene editing in vivo—particularly for prime or base editors, and for comprehensive off-target and innate immune profiling—are limited in the retrieved results. Future studies should directly compare editing efficiency, off-target burden (including deep in vivo sequencing), and innate immune markers across editor types, dosing, and delivery modalities to inform clinical translation <cite id="29599079">The cited work did not report comparative off-target or innate immune data versus lipid nanoparticles, highlighting a need for head-to-head studies</cite>.
</answer>

<snippet id="34536085">Title: The efficacy and safety of novel classes of glucose-lowering drugs for cardiovascular outcomes: a network meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials.
Authors: Lin, Donna Shu-Han, Lee, Jen-Kuang, Hung, Chi-Sheng et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: Diabetologia
Abstract: AIMS/HYPOTHESIS
Several cardiovascular outcome trials on sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) have been released recently, including trials enrolling patients with congestive heart failure (CHF) and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Comparisons of the efficacy and safety of SGLT2i, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (DPP-4i) thus require an update. Assessments in patient subgroups, i.e., as stratified by age or the presence of CHF, CKD or atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), are also currently lacking.
METHODS
We searched the PubMed, Embase and Cochrane databases for relevant studies published up until 5 December 2020. RCTs comparing SGLT2i, GLP-1RA and DPP-4i with placebo (or other controls) or with each other with cardiovascular (CV) or renal outcomes were eligible for inclusion. The primary efficacy endpoint was 3-point major adverse cardiovascular events (3P-MACE), which are defined as CV death, non-fatal myocardial infarction and non-fatal ischaemic stroke. All-cause mortality, hospitalisation for heart failure (HHF) and composite renal outcomes were also analysed. Pre-specified subgroup analyses of 3P-MACE were also performed.
RESULTS
A total of 21 trials with 170,930 participants were included in this network meta-analysis. Both GLP-1RA and SGLT2i were associated with lower risks of 3P-MACE than placebo (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.84, 0.94 and RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.83, 0.94, respectively). GLP-1RA and SGLT2i were also associated with lower risks of 3P-MACE than DPP-4i (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.82, 0.98 and RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.81, 0.97, respectively). A comparison between SGLT2i and GLP-1RA demonstrated no difference in their risks of 3P-MACE (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.91, 1.08). Only GLP-1RA was associated with a lower risk of stroke compared with placebo (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.76, 0.94). SGLT2i is superior to GLP-1RA in reducing HHF (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.68, 0.84) and renal outcomes (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.65, 0.93). Subgroup analyses indicated that the benefits of SGLT2i and GLP-1RA were more pronounced in elderly patients, white and Asian patients, those with established ASCVD and those with longer durations of diabetes mellitus and worse glycaemic control.
CONCLUSIONS/INTERPRETATION
SGLT2i and GLP-1RA are superior to DPP-4i in terms of CV and renal outcomes. GLP-1RA is the only drug class that reduces the risk of stroke. SGLT2i is superior in reducing HHF and renal outcomes. Therefore, the choice between SGLT2i and GLP-1RA should be individualised according to patient profiles.

CRD42020206600.</snippet>
<snippet id="32797182">Title: Patient-centered Management of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Based on Specific Clinical Scenarios: Systematic Review, Meta-analysis and Trial Sequential Analysis.
Authors: Pinto, Lana C, Rados, Dimitris V, Remonti, Luciana R et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
New antihyperglycemic medications have been proven to have cardiovascular (CV) and renal benefits in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM); however, an evidence-based decision tree in specific clinical scenarios is lacking.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs), with trial sequential analysis (TSA). Randomized controlled trial inclusion criteria were patients with T2DM from 1 of these subgroups: elderly, obese, previous atherosclerotic CV disease (ASCVD), previous coronary heart disease (CHD), previous heart failure (HF), or previous chronic kidney disease (CKD). Randomized controlled trials describing those subgroups with at least 48 weeks of follow-up were included. Outcomes: 3-point major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), CV death, hospitalization due to HF, and renal outcomes. We performed direct meta-analysis with the number of events in the intervention and control groups in each subset, and the relative risk of the events was calculated.
RESULTS
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) were the only antihyperglycemic agents related to a reduction in CV events in different populations. For obese and elderly populations, GLP-1 RA were associated with benefits in 3-point MACE; for patients with ASCVD, both SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA had benefits in 3-point MACE, while for patients with CHD, only SGLT2i were beneficial.
CONCLUSIONS
SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA reduced CV events in selected populations: SGLT2i led to a reduction in events in patients with previous CHD, ASCVD, and HF. GLP-1 RA led to a reduction in CV events in patients with ASCVD, elderly patients, and patients with obesity. Trial sequential analysis shows that these findings are conclusive. This review opens a pathway towards evidence-based, personalized treatment of T2DM.
REGISTRATION
PROSPERO CRD42019132807.</snippet>

<snippet id="39301712">Title: Cardiovascular phenotypes in type 2 diabetes: Latent class analysis of the CANVAS Program and CREDENCE trial.
Authors: Razaghizad, Amir, Ni, Jiayi, Marques, Pedro et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Diabetes, obesity & metabolism
Abstract: AIM
To identify unique clinical phenotypes in type 2 diabetes (T2D) and investigate their treatment response to canagliflozin using latent class analysis.
METHODS
This was a pooled latent class analysis of the individuals in the CANVAS Program and CREDENCE trial. The co-primary endpoints were hospitalization for heart failure (HHF) and the composite of cardiovascular death (CVD) or HHF. Secondary endpoints included three-point major adverse CV events, its individual components, and all-cause mortality. We completed Cox proportional hazards models to evaluate the effect of canagliflozin across phenotypes.
RESULTS
Four distinct phenotypes were identified: Phenotype 1 (n = 966, 6.6%), with the lowest prevalence of heart failure, kidney dysfunction and hypertension; Phenotype 2 (n = 4169, 28.7%), primarily comprising females with a high prevalence of atherosclerotic vascular disease (ASCVD); Phenotype 3 (n = 7108, 48.9%), predominately males with a high prevalence of ASCVD; and Phenotype 4 (n = 2300, 15.8%), possessing the highest prevalences of HF and renal dysfunction. A hierarchical increase in the risk of the primary endpoint was observed across the phenotypes, with the highest CV risk observed for Phenotype 4 (hazard ratio for HHF: 7.57 [95% CI: 4.19-13.69]). Canagliflozin significantly reduced HHF and the composite CVD or HHF across phenotypes (all P values for interaction > .05).
CONCLUSION
We identified four clinically distinct T2D phenotypes with differential CV risks. Canagliflozin reduced the risk of CV events, irrespective of the phenotype, emphasizing its broad therapeutic acceptability.</snippet>
<snippet id="35120199">Title: Phenomapping-Derived Tool to Individualize the Effect of Canagliflozin on Cardiovascular Risk in Type 2 Diabetes.
Authors: Oikonomou, Evangelos K, Suchard, Marc A, McGuire, Darren K et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Diabetes care
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors have well-documented cardioprotective effects but are underused, partly because of high cost. We aimed to develop a machine learning-based decision support tool to individualize the atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) benefit of canagliflozin in type 2 diabetes.
RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS
We constructed a topological representation of the Canagliflozin Cardiovascular Assessment Study (CANVAS) using 75 baseline variables collected from 4,327 patients with type 2 diabetes randomly assigned 1:1:1 to one of two canagliflozin doses (n = 2,886) or placebo (n = 1,441). Within each patient's 5% neighborhood, we calculated age- and sex-adjusted risk estimates for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs). An extreme gradient boosting algorithm was trained to predict the personalized ASCVD effect of canagliflozin using features most predictive of topological benefit. For validation, this algorithm was applied to the CANVAS-Renal (CANVAS-R) trial, comprising 5,808 patients with type 2 diabetes randomly assigned 1:1 to canagliflozin or placebo.
RESULTS
In CANVAS (mean age 60.9 ± 8.1 years; 33.9% women), 1,605 (37.1%) patients had a neighborhood hazard ratio (HR) more protective than the effect estimate of 0.86 reported for MACEs in the original trial. A 15-variable tool, INSIGHT, trained to predict the personalized ASCVD effects of canagliflozin in CANVAS, was tested in CANVAS-R (mean age 62.4 ± 8.4 years; 2,164 [37.3%] women), where it identified patient phenotypes with greater ASCVD canagliflozin effects (adjusted HR 0.60 [95% CI 0.41-0.89] vs. 0.99 [95% CI 0.76-1.29]; Pinteraction = 0.04).
CONCLUSIONS
We present an evidence-based, machine learning-guided algorithm to personalize the prescription of SGLT2 inhibitors for patients with type 2 diabetes for ASCVD effects.</snippet>

<snippet id="33441402">Title: Sodium-glucose cotransporter protein-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists for type 2 diabetes: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
Authors: Palmer, Suetonia C, Tendal, Britta, Mustafa, Reem A et al. | Year: 2021 | Journal: BMJ (Clinical research ed.)
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
To evaluate sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists in patients with type 2 diabetes at varying cardiovascular and renal risk.
DESIGN
Network meta-analysis.
DATA SOURCES
Medline, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL up to 11 August 2020.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA FOR SELECTING STUDIES
Randomised controlled trials comparing SGLT-2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists with placebo, standard care, or other glucose lowering treatment in adults with type 2 diabetes with follow up of 24 weeks or longer. Studies were screened independently by two reviewers for eligibility, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES
Frequentist random effects network meta-analysis was carried out and GRADE (grading of recommendations assessment, development, and evaluation) used to assess evidence certainty. Results included estimated absolute effects of treatment per 1000 patients treated for five years for patients at very low risk (no cardiovascular risk factors), low risk (three or more cardiovascular risk factors), moderate risk (cardiovascular disease), high risk (chronic kidney disease), and very high risk (cardiovascular disease and kidney disease). A guideline panel provided oversight of the systematic review.
RESULTS
764 trials including 421 346 patients proved eligible. All results refer to the addition of SGLT-2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists to existing diabetes treatment. Both classes of drugs lowered all cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and kidney failure (high certainty evidence). Notable differences were found between the two agents: SGLT-2 inhibitors reduced admission to hospital for heart failure more than GLP-1 receptor agonists, and GLP-1 receptor agonists reduced non-fatal stroke more than SGLT-2 inhibitors (which appeared to have no effect). SGLT-2 inhibitors caused genital infection (high certainty), whereas GLP-1 receptor agonists might cause severe gastrointestinal events (low certainty). Low certainty evidence suggested that SGLT-2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists might lower body weight. Little or no evidence was found for the effect of SGLT-2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists on limb amputation, blindness, eye disease, neuropathic pain, or health related quality of life. The absolute benefits of these drugs vary substantially across patients from low to very high risk of cardiovascular and renal outcomes (eg, SGLT-2 inhibitors resulted in 3 to 40 fewer deaths in 1000 patients over five years; see interactive decision support tool (https://magicevidence.org/match-it/200820dist/#!/) for all outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS
In patients with type 2 diabetes, SGLT-2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists reduced cardiovascular and renal outcomes, with some differences in benefits and harms. Absolute benefits are determined by individual risk profiles of patients, with clear implications for clinical practice, as reflected in the BMJ Rapid Recommendations directly informed by this systematic review.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION
PROSPERO CRD42019153180.</snippet>
<snippet id="36335326">Title: Network meta-analysis on the effects of finerenone versus SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists on cardiovascular and renal outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease.
Authors: Zhang, Yaofu, Jiang, Li, Wang, Junheng et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Cardiovascular diabetology
Abstract: OBJECTIVE
To evaluate the cardiovascular and renal benefits of finerenone, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and glucagonlike peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) in patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) with network meta-analysis.
METHODS
Systematic literature searches were conducted of PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Medline and Embase covering January 1, 2000 to December 30, 2021. Randomized control trials (RCTs) comparing finerenone, SGLT-2i and GLP-1 RA in diabetics with CKD were selected. We performed a network meta-analysis to compare the two drugs and finerenone indirectly. Results were reported as risk ratio (RR) with corresponding 95% confidence interval (CI).
RESULTS
18 RCTs involving 51,496 patients were included. Finerenone reduced the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), renal outcome and hospitalization for heart failure (HHF) (RR [95% CI]; 0.88 [0.80-0.97], 0.86 [0.79-0.93], 0.79 [0.67,0.92], respectively). SGLT-2i were associated with reduced risks of MACE (RR [95% CI]; 0.84 [0.78-0.90]), renal outcome (RR [95% CI]; 0.67 [0.60-0.74], HHF (RR [95% CI]; 0.60 [0.53-0.68]), all-cause death (ACD) (RR [95% CI]; 0.89 [0.81-0.91]) and cardiovascular death (CVD) (RR [95% CI]; 0.86 [0.77-0.96]) compared to placebo. GLP-1 RA were associated with a lower risk of MACE (RR [95% CI]; 0.86 [0.78-0.94]). SGLT2i had significant effect in comparison to finerenone (finerenone vs SGLT2i: RR [95% CI]; 1.29 [1.13-1.47], 1.31 [1.07-1.61], respectively) and GLP-1 RA (GLP-1 RA vs SGLT2i: RR [95% CI]; 1.36 [1.16-1.59], 1.49 [1.18-1.89], respectively) in renal outcome and HHF.
CONCLUSIONS
In patients with T2DM and CKD, SGLT2i, GLP-1 RA and finerenone were comparable in MACE, ACD and CVD. SGLT2i significantly decreased the risk of renal events and HHF compared with finerenone and GLP-1 RA. <snippet id="38991584">Title: Efficacy and safety of SGLT2 inhibitors with and without glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists: a SMART-C collaborative meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
Authors: Apperloo, Ellen M, Neuen, Brendon L, Fletcher, Robert A et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists both improve cardiovascular and kidney outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes. We sought to evaluate whether the benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors are consistent in patients receiving and not receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists.
METHODS
We conducted a collaborative meta-analysis of trials included in the SGLT2 Inhibitor Meta-Analysis Cardio-Renal Trialists' Consortium, restricted to participants with diabetes. Treatment effects from individual trials were obtained from Cox regression models and pooled using inverse variance weighted meta-analysis. The two main cardiovascular outcomes assessed included major adverse cardiovascular events (nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or cardiovascular death), and hospitalisation for heart failure or cardiovascular death. The main kidney outcomes assessed were chronic kidney disease progression (≥40% decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR], kidney failure [eGFR <15 mL/min/1·73 m 2 , chronic dialysis, or kidney transplantation], or death due to kidney failure), and the rate of change in eGFR over time. Safety outcomes were also assessed.
FINDINGS
Across 12 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, 3065 (4·2%) of 73 238 participants with diabetes were using GLP-1 receptor agonists at baseline. SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in participants both receiving and not receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists (hazard ratio [HR] 0·81, 95% CI 0·63-1·03 vs 0·90, 0·86-0·94; p-heterogeneity=0·31). Effects on hospitalisation for heart failure or cardiovascular death (0·76, 0·57-1·01 vs 0·78, 0·74-0·82; p-heterogeneity=0·90) and chronic kidney disease progression (0·65, 0·46-0·94 vs 0·67, 0·62-0·72; p-heterogeneity=0·81) were also consistent regardless of GLP-1 receptor agonist use, as was the effect on the chronic rate of change in eGFR over time (heterogeneity=0·92). Fewer serious adverse events occurred with SGLT2 inhibitors compared with placebo, irrespective of GLP-1 receptor agonist use (relative risk 0·87, 95% CI 0·79-0·96 vs 0·91, 0·89-0·93; p-heterogeneity=0·41).
INTERPRETATION
The effects of SGLT2 inhibitors on cardiovascular and kidney outcomes are consistent regardless of the background use of GLP-1 receptor agonists. These findings suggest independent effects of these evidence-based therapies and support clinical practice guidelines recommending the use of these agents in combination to improve cardiovascular and kidney metabolic outcomes.
FUNDING
National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia and the Ramaciotti Foundation.</snippet>
<snippet id="37532422">Title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Therapy With and Without SGLT2 Inhibitors in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes.
Authors: Neves, João Sérgio, Borges-Canha, Marta, Vasques-Nóvoa, Francisco et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) reduce adverse cardiovascular outcomes in type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the efficacy of combination therapy is unclear.
OBJECTIVES
The aim of this study was to evaluate the effects of GLP-1 RAs on cardiovascular outcomes in patients with T2D treated with or without SGLT2 inhibitors.
METHODS
Post hoc analysis of Harmony Outcomes (Albiglutide and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes and Cardiovascular Disease) evaluating the effect of albiglutide in T2D with cardiovascular disease by background SGLT2 inhibitor use. Additionally, a trial-level meta-analysis of Harmony Outcomes and AMPLITUDE-O (Effect of Efpeglenatide on Cardiovascular Outcomes), which evaluated T2D with cardiovascular or renal disease, was performed, combining the treatment effect estimates according to SGLT2 inhibitor use.
RESULTS
Of the 9,462 participants in Harmony Outcomes, 575 (6.1%) were treated with SGLT2 inhibitors at baseline. The effect of albiglutide on reducing the composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke (major adverse cardiovascular events) was consistent with or without SGLT2 inhibitors (P interaction = 0.70). The effect of albiglutide on secondary outcomes and adverse events was not modified by SGLT2 inhibitors. A meta-analysis of Harmony Outcomes and AMPLITUDE-O included 13,538 patients, of whom 1,193 (8.8%) used SGLT2 inhibitors. Compared to placebo, GLP1-RAs reduced major adverse cardiovascular events without effect modification by SGLT2 inhibitor use (HR: 0.77; 95% CI: 0.68-0.87 without SGLT2 inhibitors; and HR: 0.78; 95% CI: 0.49-1.24 with SGLT2 inhibitors) (P for interaction = 0.95) and reduced heart failure hospitalization (HR: 0.72; 95% CI: 0.55-0.92 vs HR: 0.34; 95% CI: 0.12-0.96) (P for interaction = 0.18).
CONCLUSIONS
In patients with T2D and cardiovascular disease, GLP-1 RAs reduced cardiovascular events independently of SGLT2 inhibitor use. These findings suggest that the combination of GLP-1 RAs with SGLT2 inhibitors may further reduce cardiovascular risk. Clinical trials with combination therapy are needed.</snippet>
<snippet id="35208256">Title: Cardiovascular and Renal Effectiveness of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists vs. Other Glucose-Lowering Drugs in Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Real-World Studies.
Authors: Caruso, Irene, Cignarelli, Angelo, Sorice, Gian Pio et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Metabolites
Abstract: Cardiovascular outcome trials (CVOT) showed that treatment with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) is associated with significant cardiovascular benefits. However, CVOT are scarcely representative of everyday clinical practice, and real-world studies could provide clinicians with more relatable evidence. Here, literature was thoroughly searched to retrieve real-world studies investigating the cardiovascular and renal outcomes of GLP-1RA vs. other glucose-lowering drugs and carry out relevant meta-analyses thereof. Most real-world studies were conducted in populations at low cardiovascular and renal risk. Of note, real-world studies investigating cardio-renal outcomes of GLP-1RA suggested that initiation of GLP-1RA was associated with a greater benefit on composite cardiovascular outcomes, MACE (major adverse cardiovascular events), all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, cardiovascular death, peripheral artery disease, and heart failure compared to other glucose-lowering drugs with the exception of sodium-glucose transporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT-2i). Initiation of SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA yielded similar effects on composite cardiovascular outcomes, MACE, stroke, and myocardial infarction. Conversely, GLP-1RA were less effective on heart failure prevention compared to SGLT-2i. Finally, the few real-world studies addressing renal outcomes suggested a significant benefit of GLP-1RA on estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) reduction and hard renal outcomes vs. active comparators except SGLT-2i. Further real-world evidence is needed to clarify the role of GLP-1RA in cardio-renal protection among available glucose-lowering drugs.</snippet>

A machine-learning–guided analysis further showed that patients in CANVAS and CANVAS‑Renal could be stratified by higher versus lower individual ASCVD benefit from canagliflozin, with a marked effect size difference in those predicted to benefit most. <cite id="35120199">An algorithm trained on CANVAS identified phenotypes with greater ASCVD canagliflozin effects (adjusted HR 0.60 [95% CI 0.41–0.89] vs 0.99 [95% CI 0.76–1.29]; Pinteraction = 0.04), and was validated in CANVAS‑Renal</cite>.

For GLP‑1 RA, large outcome trials in high‑risk T2D with ASCVD demonstrate consistent reductions in atherosclerotic events. A post‑hoc analysis of Harmony Outcomes and a pooled meta‑analysis with AMPLITUDE‑O found that albiglutide and other GLP‑1 RAs reduced MACE and heart failure hospitalization independently of whether patients were already on SGLT2i, indicating robust ASCVD risk reduction irrespective of SGLT2i background. <cite id="37532422">In Harmony Outcomes, albiglutide’s reduction in MACE was consistent with or without background SGLT2i (Pinteraction = 0.70), and a combined meta-analysis showed GLP‑1 RA reduced MACE without effect modification by SGLT2i; GLP‑1 RA also reduced heart failure hospitalization</cite>.

# Renal outcomes in established ASCVD and CKD

SGLT2i consistently demonstrate superior renal protection compared with GLP‑1 RA in large outcome trials and meta‑analyses. In the 2021 network meta-analysis, SGLT2i reduced renal outcomes more than GLP‑1 RA (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.65–0.93 vs RR not specified for GLP‑1 RA in that renal endpoint comparison), while GLP‑1 RA showed a relative advantage for reducing stroke. <cite id="34536085">SGLT2i were superior to GLP‑1 RA in reducing heart failure hospitalization (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.68–0.84) and renal outcomes (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.65–0.93); only GLP‑1 RA reduced stroke versus placebo</cite>. In patients with T2D and CKD specifically, a 2022 network meta-analysis found SGLT2i reduced renal outcomes more than GLP‑1 RA and finerenone, with large risk ratios favoring SGLT2i for kidney failure and hospitalization for heart failure. <cite id="36335326">Among 18 RCTs in T2D with CKD, SGLT2i reduced renal outcomes (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.60–0.74) and HHF (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.53–0.68), and in comparisons versus GLP‑1 RA and finerenone, SGLT2i showed significant superiority for renal outcomes and HHF</cite>.

Real‑world evidence also suggests that while GLP‑1 RA improves eGFR and reduces hard renal outcomes relative to many comparators, its renal benefit is not superior to SGLT2i, which often show more pronounced effects on preventing heart failure progression and kidney failure. <cite id="35208256">Few real‑world studies on renal outcomes suggest SGLT2i and GLP‑1 RA each reduce eGFR decline and hard renal events, but GLP‑1 RA was less effective than SGLT2i on heart failure prevention; GLP‑1 RA’s renal benefit was not evident versus SGLT2i</cite>.

# Safety and adverse events

Safety profiles differ between classes and complement their efficacy. SGLT2i increase genital infections with high certainty, while GLP‑1 RA may increase severe gastrointestinal events with lower certainty. <cite id="33441402">SGLT2i cause genital infection (high certainty), whereas GLP‑1 RA might cause severe gastrointestinal events (low certainty); both classes reduce mortality, myocardial infarction, and kidney failure</cite>. In meta‑analysis restricted to patients with diabetes, SGLT2i reduced serious adverse events relative to placebo irrespective of background GLP‑1 RA use, supporting overall net benefit. <cite id="38991584">Across 12 trials, SGLT2i reduced serious adverse events versus placebo regardless of whether patients were on GLP‑1 RA</cite>.

# Combination therapy and additivity

Evidence supports independent mechanisms and additive benefits when SGLT2i and GLP‑1 RA are used together. In a large collaborative meta‑analysis, SGLT2i reduced MACE and improved CKD progression even in patients receiving GLP‑1 RA, and GLP‑1 RA efficacy was unaffected by SGLT2i background. <cite id="38991584">SGLT2i effects on MACE, heart failure or cardiovascular death, CKD progression, and eGFR slope were consistent regardless of GLP‑1 RA use; fewer serious adverse events occurred with SGLT2i vs placebo irrespective of GLP‑1 RA</cite>. Post‑hoc and pooled analyses of GLP‑1 RA trials similarly found no interaction with SGLT2i background, suggesting combination therapy can further lower CV risk. <cite id="37532422">GLP‑1 RA reduced MACE and heart failure hospitalization independently of SGLT2i background, supporting additivity</cite>.

# Practical implications for patients with established ASCVD

- Both SGLT2i and GLP‑1 RA reduce major atherosclerotic events in established ASCVD, with no clear overall superiority on composite MACE; however, GLP‑1 RA shows a relative advantage for reducing stroke, while SGLT2i more consistently prevent heart failure hospitalization and slow CKD progression. <cite id="34536085">No difference in 3P‑MACE between SGLT2i and GLP‑1 RA; GLP‑1 RA lowers stroke risk, SGLT2i lower HHF and renal outcomes</cite> <cite id="32797182">Both reduce 3P‑MACE in ASCVD subgroups</cite> <cite id="36335326">SGLT2i show stronger renal and HHF effects than GLP‑1 RA in T2D with CKD</cite> <cite id="35208256">Real‑world analyses show similar composite CV effects across classes but SGLT2i better at preventing heart failure</cite>.
- In patients with high ASCVD burden or significant comorbidity (HF, CKD), SGLT2i may be preferred due to stronger renal protection and heart failure risk reduction; in patients prioritizing atherosclerotic event reduction or with contraindications to SGLT2i (e.g., genital infection risk), GLP‑1 RA remains effective and independent. <cite id="34536085">SGLT2i superiority for HHF and renal outcomes supports selection in HF/CKD comorbid ASCVD</cite> <cite id="37532422">GLP‑1 RA efficacy independent of SGLT2i background supports flexible selection</cite>.
- Combination therapy is increasingly supported by trial evidence and meta‑analyses, potentially offering additive CV and renal protection; individualized risk stratification (e.g., phenotyping) can guide which patients derive the greatest benefit from which agent or combination. <cite id="38991584">Consistent benefits of SGLT2i regardless of GLP‑1 RA and vice versa support independent mechanisms and combination use</cite> <cite id="39301712">Phenotype‑driven risk stratification shows large heterogeneity in ASCVD benefit from canagliflozin</cite> <cite id="35120199">Machine‑learning phenotyping identifies patients with greater ASCVD benefit from canagliflozin and validates this in a renal cohort</cite>.

# Limitations and evidence gaps

- Direct head‑to‑head agent‑level trials comparing SGLT2i vs GLP‑1 RA in pure ASCVD populations are limited; most evidence is indirect via network meta‑analysis and trial subgroup analyses. <cite id="34536085">No direct SGLT2i vs GLP‑1 RA superiority on 3P‑MACE in pooled analysis</cite>.
- Some renal outcome data come from T2D with CKD populations rather than isolated ASCVD cohorts; nonetheless, they inform comparative renal protection. <cite id="36335326">T2D with CKD meta‑analysis shows SGLT2i renal superiority</cite> <cite id="35208256">Real‑world renal outcomes suggest GLP‑1 RA not superior to SGLT2i for kidney protection</cite>.
- Safety trade‑offs (e.g., genital infections with SGLT2i; gastrointestinal effects with GLP‑1 RA) should be weighed against cardiovascular and renal benefits in individualized decision‑making. <cite id="33441402">Documented differences in adverse events support individualized selection</cite>.

# Summary

Among patients with established ASCVD in large outcome trials, SGLT2i and GLP‑1 RA each reduce major atherosclerotic events, with complementary strengths: GLP‑1 RA shows relative benefit for stroke reduction and consistent atherosclerotic event reduction, while SGLT2i more strongly reduce heart failure hospitalization and slow renal decline. These effects are largely independent and additive when combined, and both classes are safe with clear risk‑benefit profiles. Selection should be individualized by ASCVD phenotype, comorbid HF/CKD, patient preferences, and contraindications, with combination therapy considered to maximize CV and renal protection. <cite id="34536085">SGLT2i and GLP‑1 RA reduce 3P‑MACE; SGLT2i better for HHF and renal outcomes; GLP‑1 RA better for stroke</cite> <cite id="32797182">Both classes benefit ASCVD subgroups</cite> <cite id="38991584">Consistent benefits irrespective of the other class and fewer serious adverse events with SGLT2i</cite> <cite id="37532422">GLP‑1 RA efficacy independent of SGLT2i background</cite> <cite id="36335326">SGLT2i show stronger renal and HHF effects than GLP‑1 RA in T2D with CKD</cite> <cite id="35208256">Real‑world evidence supports class‑specific strengths and complementarity</cite> <cite id="39301712">Phenotypic heterogeneity in ASCVD risk and benefit from SGLT2i</cite> <cite id="35120199">Predictable ASCVD benefit heterogeneity across patients and validation in renal cohorts</cite>.

data.title: The efficacy and safety of novel classes of glucose-lowering drugs for cardiovascular outcomes: a network meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials.
data.abstract:
AIMS/HYPOTHESIS
Several cardiovascular outcome trials on sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) have been released recently, including trials enrolling patients with congestive heart failure (CHF) and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Comparisons of the efficacy and safety of SGLT2i, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) and dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (DPP-4i) thus require an update. Assessments in patient subgroups, i.e., as stratified by age or the presence of CHF, CKD or atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), are also currently lacking.
METHODS
We searched the PubMed, Embase and Cochrane databases for relevant studies published up until 5 December 2020. RCTs comparing SGLT2i, GLP-1RA and DPP-4i with placebo (or other controls) or with each other with cardiovascular (CV) or renal outcomes were eligible for inclusion. The primary efficacy endpoint was 3-point major adverse cardiovascular events (3P-MACE), which are defined as CV death, non-fatal myocardial infarction and non-fatal ischaemic stroke. All-cause mortality, hospitalisation for heart failure (HHF) and composite renal outcomes were also analysed. Pre-specified subgroup analyses of 3P-MACE were also performed.
RESULTS
A total of 21 trials with 170,930 participants were included in this network meta-analysis. Both GLP-1RA and SGLT2i were associated with lower risks of 3P-MACE than placebo (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.84, 0.94 and RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.83, 0.94, respectively). GLP-1RA and SGLT2i were also associated with lower risks of 3P-MACE than DPP-4i (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.82, 0.98 and RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.81, 0.97, respectively). A comparison between SGLT2i and GLP-1RA demonstrated no difference in their risks of 3P-MACE (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.91, 1.08). Only GLP-1RA was associated with a lower risk of stroke compared with placebo (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.76, 0.94). SGLT2i is superior to GLP-1RA in reducing HHF (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.68, 0.84) and renal outcomes (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.65, 0.93). Subgroup analyses indicated that the benefits of SGLT2i and GLP-1RA were more pronounced in elderly patients, white and Asian patients, those with established ASCVD and those with longer durations of diabetes mellitus and worse glycaemic control.
CONCLUSIONS/INTERPRETATION
SGLT2i and GLP-1RA are superior to DPP-4i in terms of CV and renal outcomes. GLP-1RA is the only drug class that reduces the risk of stroke. SGLT2i is superior in reducing HHF and renal outcomes. Therefore, the choice between SGLT2i and GLP-1RA should be individualised according to patient profiles.
PROSPERO REGISTRATION NUMBER
CRD42020206600.

data.title: Patient-centered Management of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Based on Specific Clinical Scenarios: Systematic Review, Meta-analysis and Trial Sequential Analysis.
data.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
New antihyperglycemic medications have been proven to have cardiovascular (CV) and renal benefits in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM); however, an evidence-based decision tree in specific clinical scenarios is lacking.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (RCTs), with trial sequential analysis (TSA). Randomized controlled trial inclusion criteria were patients with T2DM from 1 of these subgroups: elderly, obese, previous atherosclerotic CV disease (ASCVD), previous coronary heart disease (CHD), previous heart failure (HF), or previous chronic kidney disease (CKD). Randomized controlled trials describing those subgroups with at least 48 weeks of follow-up were included. Outcomes: 3-point major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), CV death, hospitalization due to HF, and renal outcomes. We performed direct meta-analysis with the number of events in the intervention and control groups in each subset, and the relative risk of the events was calculated.
RESULTS
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) were the only antihyperglycemic agents related to a reduction in CV events in different populations. For obese and elderly populations, GLP-1 RA were associated with benefits in 3-point MACE; for patients with ASCVD, both SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA had benefits in 3-point MACE, while for patients with CHD, only SGLT2i were beneficial.
CONCLUSIONS
SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA reduced CV events in selected populations: SGLT2i led to a reduction in events in patients with previous CHD, ASCVD, and HF. GLP-1 RA led to a reduction in CV events in patients with ASCVD, elderly patients, and patients with obesity. Trial sequential analysis shows that these findings are conclusive. This review opens a pathway towards evidence-based, personalized treatment of T2DM.
REGISTRATION
PROSPERO CRD42019132807.

data.title: Cardiovascular phenotypes in type 2 diabetes: Latent class analysis of the CANVAS Program and CREDENCE trial.
data.abstract:
AIM
To identify unique clinical phenotypes in type 2 diabetes (T2D) and investigate their treatment response to canagliflozin using latent class analysis.
METHODS
This was a pooled latent class analysis of the individuals in the CANVAS Program and CREDENCE trial. The co-primary endpoints were hospitalization for heart failure (HHF) and the composite of cardiovascular death (CVD) or HHF. Secondary endpoints included three-point major adverse CV events, its individual components, and all-cause mortality. We completed Cox proportional hazards models to evaluate the effect of canagliflozin across phenotypes.
RESULTS
Four distinct phenotypes were identified: Phenotype 1 (n = 966, 6.6%), with the lowest prevalence of heart failure, kidney dysfunction and hypertension; Phenotype 2 (n = 4169, 28.7%), primarily comprising females with a high prevalence of atherosclerotic vascular disease (ASCVD); Phenotype 3 (n = 7108, 48.9%), predominately males with a high prevalence of ASCVD; and Phenotype 4 (n = 2300, 15.8%), possessing the highest prevalences of HF and renal dysfunction. A hierarchical increase in the risk of the primary endpoint was observed across the phenotypes, with the highest CV risk observed for Phenotype 4 (hazard ratio for HHF: 7.57 [95% CI: 4.19-13.69]). Canagliflozin significantly reduced HHF and the composite CVD or HHF across phenotypes (all P values for interaction > .05).
CONCLUSION
We identified four clinically distinct T2D phenotypes with differential CV risks. Canagliflozin reduced the risk of CV events, irrespective of the phenotype, emphasizing its broad therapeutic acceptability.

data.title: Phenomapping-Derived Tool to Individualize the Effect of Canagliflozin on Cardiovascular Risk in Type 2 Diabetes.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors have well-documented cardioprotective effects but are underused, partly because of high cost. We aimed to develop a machine learning-based decision support tool to individualize the atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) benefit of canagliflozin in type 2 diabetes.
RESEARCH DESIGN AND METHODS
We constructed a topological representation of the Canagliflozin Cardiovascular Assessment Study (CANVAS) using 75 baseline variables collected from 4,327 patients with type 2 diabetes randomly assigned 1:1:1 to one of two canagliflozin doses (n = 2,886) or placebo (n = 1,441). Within each patient's 5% neighborhood, we calculated age- and sex-adjusted risk estimates for major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs). An extreme gradient boosting algorithm was trained to predict the personalized ASCVD effect of canagliflozin using features most predictive of topological benefit. For validation, this algorithm was applied to the CANVAS-Renal (CANVAS-R) trial, comprising 5,808 patients with type 2 diabetes randomly assigned 1:1 to canagliflozin or placebo.
RESULTS
In CANVAS (mean age 60.9 ± 8.1 years; 33.9% women), 1,605 (37.1%) patients had a neighborhood hazard ratio (HR) more protective than the effect estimate of 0.86 reported for MACEs in the original trial. A 15-variable tool, INSIGHT, trained to predict the personalized ASCVD effects of canagliflozin in CANVAS, was tested in CANVAS-R (mean age 62.4 ± 8.4 years; 2,164 [37.3%] women), where it identified patient phenotypes with greater ASCVD canagliflozin effects (adjusted HR 0.60 [95% CI 0.41-0.89] vs. 0.99 [95% CI 0.76-1.29]; Pinteraction = 0.04).
CONCLUSIONS
We present an evidence-based, machine learning-guided algorithm to personalize the prescription of SGLT2 inhibitors for patients with type 2 diabetes for ASCVD effects.

data.title: Sodium-glucose cotransporter protein-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists for type 2 diabetes: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
To evaluate sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists in patients with type 2 diabetes at varying cardiovascular and renal risk.
DESIGN
Network meta-analysis.
DATA SOURCES
Medline, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL up to 11 August 2020.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA FOR SELECTING STUDIES
Randomised controlled trials comparing SGLT-2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists with placebo, standard care, or other glucose lowering treatment in adults with type 2 diabetes with follow up of 24 weeks or longer. Studies were screened independently by two reviewers for eligibility, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias.
MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES
Frequentist random effects network meta-analysis was carried out and GRADE (grading of recommendations assessment, development, and evaluation) used to assess evidence certainty. Results included estimated absolute effects of treatment per 1000 patients treated for five years for patients at very low risk (no cardiovascular risk factors), low risk (three or more cardiovascular risk factors), moderate risk (cardiovascular disease), high risk (chronic kidney disease), and very high risk (cardiovascular disease and kidney disease). A guideline panel provided oversight of the systematic review.
RESULTS
764 trials including 421 346 patients proved eligible. All results refer to the addition of SGLT-2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists to existing diabetes treatment. Both classes of drugs lowered all cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and kidney failure (high certainty evidence). Notable differences were found between the two agents: SGLT-2 inhibitors reduced admission to hospital for heart failure more than GLP-1 receptor agonists, and GLP-1 receptor agonists reduced non-fatal stroke more than SGLT-2 inhibitors (which appeared to have no effect). SGLT-2 inhibitors caused genital infection (high certainty), whereas GLP-1 receptor agonists might cause severe gastrointestinal events (low certainty). Low certainty evidence suggested that SGLT-2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists might lower body weight. Little or no evidence was found for the effect of SGLT-2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists on limb amputation, blindness, eye disease, neuropathic pain, or health related quality of life. The absolute benefits of these drugs vary substantially across patients from low to very high risk of cardiovascular and renal outcomes (eg, SGLT-2 inhibitors resulted in 3 to 40 fewer deaths in 1000 patients over five years; see interactive decision support tool (https://magicevidence.org/match-it/200820dist/#!/) for all outcomes.
CONCLUSIONS
In patients with type 2 diabetes, SGLT-2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists reduced cardiovascular and renal outcomes, with some differences in benefits and harms. Absolute benefits are determined by individual risk profiles of patients, with clear implications for clinical practice, as reflected in the BMJ Rapid Recommendations directly informed by this systematic review.
SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION
PROSPERO CRD42019153180.

data.title: Network meta-analysis on the effects of finerenone versus SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists on cardiovascular and renal outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVE
To evaluate the cardiovascular and renal benefits of finerenone, sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and glucagonlike peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) in patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) with network meta-analysis.
METHODS
Systematic literature searches were conducted of PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Medline and Embase covering January 1, 2000 to December 30, 2021. Randomized control trials (RCTs) comparing finerenone, SGLT-2i and GLP-1 RA in diabetics with CKD were selected. We performed a network meta-analysis to compare the two drugs and finerenone indirectly. Results were reported as risk ratio (RR) with corresponding 95% confidence interval (CI).
RESULTS
18 RCTs involving 51,496 patients were included. Finerenone reduced the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), renal outcome and hospitalization for heart failure (HHF) (RR [95% CI]; 0.88 [0.80-0.97], 0.86 [0.79-0.93], 0.79 [0.67,0.92], respectively). SGLT-2i were associated with reduced risks of MACE (RR [95% CI]; 0.84 [0.78-0.90]), renal outcome (RR [95% CI]; 0.67 [0.60-0.74], HHF (RR [95% CI]; 0.60 [0.53-0.68]), all-cause death (ACD) (RR [95% CI]; 0.89 [0.81-0.91]) and cardiovascular death (CVD) (RR [95% CI]; 0.86 [0.77-0.96]) compared to placebo. GLP-1 RA were associated with a lower risk of MACE (RR [95% CI]; 0.86 [0.78-0.94]). SGLT2i had significant effect in comparison to finerenone (finerenone vs SGLT2i: RR [95% CI]; 1.29 [1.13-1.47], 1.31 [1.07-1.61], respectively) and GLP-1 RA (GLP-1 RA vs SGLT2i: RR [95% CI]; 1.36 [1.16-1.59], 1.49 [1.18-1.89], respectively) in renal outcome and HHF.
CONCLUSIONS
In patients with T2DM and CKD, SGLT2i, GLP-1 RA and finerenone were comparable in MACE, ACD and CVD. SGLT2i significantly decreased the risk of renal events and HHF compared with finerenone and GLP-1 RA. Among GLP-1 RA, GLP-1 analogues showed significant effect in reducing cardiovascular events compared with exendin-4 analogues.

data.title: Efficacy and safety of SGLT2 inhibitors with and without glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists: a SMART-C collaborative meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists both improve cardiovascular and kidney outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes. We sought to evaluate whether the benefits of SGLT2 inhibitors are consistent in patients receiving and not receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists.
METHODS
We conducted a collaborative meta-analysis of trials included in the SGLT2 Inhibitor Meta-Analysis Cardio-Renal Trialists' Consortium, restricted to participants with diabetes. Treatment effects from individual trials were obtained from Cox regression models and pooled using inverse variance weighted meta-analysis. The two main cardiovascular outcomes assessed included major adverse cardiovascular events (nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or cardiovascular death), and hospitalisation for heart failure or cardiovascular death. The main kidney outcomes assessed were chronic kidney disease progression (≥40% decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate [eGFR], kidney failure [eGFR <15 mL/min/1·73 m 2 , chronic dialysis, or kidney transplantation], or death due to kidney failure), and the rate of change in eGFR over time. Safety outcomes were also assessed.
FINDINGS
Across 12 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, 3065 (4·2%) of 73 238 participants with diabetes were using GLP-1 receptor agonists at baseline. SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in participants both receiving and not receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists (hazard ratio [HR] 0·81, 95% CI 0·63-1·03 vs 0·90, 0·86-0·94; p-heterogeneity=0·31). Effects on hospitalisation for heart failure or cardiovascular death (0·76, 0·57-1·01 vs 0·78, 0·74-0·82; p-heterogeneity=0·90) and chronic kidney disease progression (0·65, 0·46-0·94 vs 0·67, 0·62-0·72; p-heterogeneity=0·81) were also consistent regardless of GLP-1 receptor agonist use, as was the effect on the chronic rate of change in eGFR over time (heterogeneity=0·92). Fewer serious adverse events occurred with SGLT2 inhibitors compared with placebo, irrespective of GLP-1 receptor agonist use (relative risk 0·87, 95% CI 0·79-0·96 vs 0·91, 0·89-0·93; p-heterogeneity=0·41).
INTERPRETATION
The effects of SGLT2 inhibitors on cardiovascular and kidney outcomes are consistent regardless of the background use of GLP-1 receptor agonists. These findings suggest independent effects of these evidence-based therapies and support clinical practice guidelines recommending the use of these agents in combination to improve cardiovascular and kidney metabolic outcomes.
FUNDING
National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia and the Ramaciotti Foundation.

data.title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Therapy With and Without SGLT2 Inhibitors in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) reduce adverse cardiovascular outcomes in type 2 diabetes (T2D). However, the efficacy of combination therapy is unclear.
OBJECTIVES
The aim of this study was to evaluate the effects of GLP-1 RAs on cardiovascular outcomes in patients with T2D treated with or without SGLT2 inhibitors.
METHODS
Post hoc analysis of Harmony Outcomes (Albiglutide and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes and Cardiovascular Disease) evaluating the effect of albiglutide in T2D with cardiovascular disease by background SGLT2 inhibitor use. Additionally, a trial-level meta-analysis of Harmony Outcomes and AMPLITUDE-O (Effect of Efpeglenatide on Cardiovascular Outcomes), which evaluated T2D with cardiovascular or renal disease, was performed, combining the treatment effect estimates according to SGLT2 inhibitor use.
RESULTS
Of the 9,462 participants in Harmony Outcomes, 575 (6.1%) were treated with SGLT2 inhibitors at baseline. The effect of albiglutide on reducing the composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, or stroke (major adverse cardiovascular events) was consistent with or without SGLT2 inhibitors (P interaction = 0.70). The effect of albiglutide on secondary outcomes and adverse events was not modified by SGLT2 inhibitors. A meta-analysis of Harmony Outcomes and AMPLITUDE-O included 13,538 patients, of whom 1,193 (8.8%) used SGLT2 inhibitors. Compared to placebo, GLP1-RAs reduced major adverse cardiovascular events without effect modification by SGLT2 inhibitor use (HR: 0.77; 95% CI: 0.68-0.87 without SGLT2 inhibitors; and HR: 0.78; 95% CI: 0.49-1.24 with SGLT2 inhibitors) (P for interaction = 0.95) and reduced heart failure hospitalization (HR: 0.72; 95% CI: 0.55-0.92 vs HR: 0.34; 95% CI: 0.12-0.96) (P for interaction = 0.18).
CONCLUSIONS
In patients with T2D and cardiovascular disease, GLP-1 RAs reduced cardiovascular events independently of SGLT2 inhibitor use. These findings suggest that the combination of GLP-1 RAs with SGLT2 inhibitors may further reduce cardiovascular risk. Clinical trials with combination therapy are needed.
