data.title: Cardiovascular and Renal Effectiveness of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists vs. Other Glucose-Lowering Drugs in Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Real-World Studies.
data.abstract: Cardiovascular outcome trials (CVOT) showed that treatment with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) is associated with significant cardiovascular benefits. However, CVOT are scarcely representative of everyday clinical practice, and real-world studies could provide clinicians with more relatable evidence. Here, literature was thoroughly searched to retrieve real-world studies investigating the cardiovascular and renal outcomes of GLP-1RA vs. other glucose-lowering drugs and carry out relevant meta-analyses thereof. Most real-world studies were conducted in populations at low cardiovascular and renal risk. Of note, real-world studies investigating cardio-renal outcomes of GLP-1RA suggested that initiation of GLP-1RA was associated with a greater benefit on composite cardiovascular outcomes, MACE (major adverse cardiovascular events), all-cause mortality, myocardial infarction, stroke, cardiovascular death, peripheral artery disease, and heart failure compared to other glucose-lowering drugs with the exception of sodium-glucose transporter-2 inhibitors (SGLT-2i). Initiation of SGLT-2i and GLP-1RA yielded similar effects on composite cardiovascular outcomes, MACE, stroke, and myocardial infarction. Conversely, GLP-1RA were less effective on heart failure prevention compared to SGLT-2i. Finally, the few real-world studies addressing renal outcomes suggested a significant benefit of GLP-1RA on estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) reduction and hard renal outcomes vs. active comparators except SGLT-2i. Further real-world evidence is needed to clarify the role of GLP-1RA in cardio-renal protection among available glucose-lowering drugs.

trajectory.final_answer:
# Bottom line

In patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) from large outcome trials and meta-analyses, both SGLT2 inhibitors (SGLT2i) and GLP‑1 receptor agonists (GLP‑1 RA) reduce major cardiovascular events, but they differ on specific outcomes and renal protection. SGLT2i tend to reduce heart failure hospitalization and renal events more than GLP‑1 RA, while GLP‑1 RA shows a relative advantage for reducing stroke and may have more consistent effects on atherosclerotic events across subgroups, including those with prior ASCVD. These differences are consistent across trials and meta-analyses and support class-independent benefits as well as potential additivity when used in combination. <cite id="34536085">Both GLP‑1 RA and SGLT2i lower 3‑point MACE versus placebo, with no difference between SGLT2i and GLP‑1 RA on 3P‑MACE; SGLT2i are superior for heart failure hospitalization and renal outcomes, and GLP‑1 RA is the only class showing lower stroke risk versus placebo</cite> <cite id="32797182">In subgroup analyses, benefits of SGLT2i and GLP‑1 RA on 3P‑MACE are more pronounced in patients with established ASCVD</cite> <cite id="38991584">In a collaborative meta-analysis of 12 randomized, placebo-controlled trials, SGLT2i reduced major adverse cardiovascular events and slowed CKD progression regardless of whether patients were or were not receiving background GLP‑1 RA</cite> <cite id="37532422">A post‑hoc analysis of Harmony Outcomes and a meta-analysis with AMPLITUDE‑O showed GLP‑1 RA reduced MACE and heart failure hospitalization independently of SGLT2i background use</cite> <cite id="35208256">Real‑world meta-analyses suggest GLP‑1 RA provides greater benefit on composite CV outcomes and mortality than SGLT2i, with similar effects on composite CV outcomes and MACE but less effectiveness on heart failure prevention compared to SGLT2i; renal outcomes show benefit for GLP‑1 RA versus many comparators but not SGLT2i</cite>.

# Cardiovascular outcomes in established ASCVD

Across network meta-analyses pooling large outcome trials, both SGLT2i and GLP‑1 RA reduce 3‑point MACE (cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke) versus placebo and versus dipeptidyl peptidase‑4 inhibitors (DPP‑4i), with no significant difference between SGLT2i and GLP‑1 RA on overall MACE. In subgroup analyses focused on patients with established ASCVD, the risk reduction on 3P‑MACE is pronounced for both classes. <cite id="34536085">GLP‑1 RA and SGLT2i each reduced 3P‑MACE versus placebo (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.84–0.94 and RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.83–0.94, respectively), and both were superior to DPP‑4i; head‑to‑head, SGLT2i and GLP‑1 RA had similar 3P‑MACE risk (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.91–1.08). Subgroup analyses indicated greater benefits in patients with established ASCVD</cite> <cite id="32797182">For patients with ASCVD, both SGLT2i and GLP‑1 RA reduced 3P‑MACE, reflecting benefits in this established ASCVD population</cite>.

Trial-based phenotyping in the CANVAS program (canagliflozin) identified ASCVD‑rich cohorts and confirmed robust CV risk gradients across phenotypes. Canagliflozin significantly reduced the composite of cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization and reduced heart failure hospitalization across all phenotypes, supporting broad CV protection in patients with ASCVD. <cite id="39301712">Four phenotypes were identified, including large classes with high ASCVD prevalence; canagliflozin significantly reduced heart failure hospitalization and the composite of cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization across phenotypes</cite>. A machine-learning–guided analysis further showed that patients in CANVAS and CANVAS‑Renal could be stratified by higher versus lower individual ASCVD benefit from canagliflozin, with a marked effect size difference in those predicted to benefit most. <cite id="35120199">An algorithm trained on CANVAS identified phenotypes with greater ASCVD canagliflozin effects (adjusted HR 0.60 [95% CI 0.41–0.89] vs 0.99 [95% CI 0.76–1.29]; Pinteraction = 0.04), and was validated in CANVAS‑Renal</cite>.

For GLP‑1 RA, large outcome trials in high‑risk T2D with ASCVD demonstrate consistent reductions in atherosclerotic events. A post‑hoc analysis of Harmony Outcomes and a pooled meta‑analysis with AMPLITUDE‑O found that albiglutide and other GLP‑1 RAs reduced MACE and heart failure hospitalization independently of whether patients were already on SGLT2i, indicating robust ASCVD risk reduction irrespective of SGLT2i background. <cite id="37532422">In Harmony Outcomes, albiglutide’s reduction in MACE was consistent with or without background SGLT2i (Pinteraction = 0.70), and a combined meta-analysis showed GLP‑1 RA reduced MACE without effect modification by SGLT2i; GLP‑1 RA also reduced heart failure hospitalization</cite>.

# Renal outcomes in established ASCVD and CKD

SGLT2i consistently demonstrate superior renal protection compared with GLP‑1 RA in large outcome trials and meta‑analyses. In the 2021 network meta-analysis, SGLT2i reduced renal outcomes more than GLP‑1 RA (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.65–0.93 vs RR not specified for GLP‑1 RA in that renal endpoint comparison), while GLP‑1 RA showed a relative advantage for reducing stroke. <cite id="34536085">SGLT2i were superior to GLP‑1 RA in reducing heart failure hospitalization (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.68–0.84) and renal outcomes (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.65–0.93); only GLP‑1 RA reduced stroke versus placebo</cite>. In patients with T2D and CKD specifically, a 2022 network meta-analysis found SGLT2i reduced renal outcomes more than GLP‑1 RA and finerenone, with large risk ratios favoring SGLT2i for kidney failure and hospitalization for heart failure. <cite id="36335326">Among 18 RCTs in T2D with CKD, SGLT2i reduced renal outcomes (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.60–0.74) and HHF (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.53–0.68), and in comparisons versus GLP‑1 RA and finerenone, SGLT2i showed significant superiority for renal outcomes and HHF</cite>.

Real‑world evidence also suggests that while GLP‑1 RA improves eGFR and reduces hard renal outcomes relative to many comparators, its renal benefit is not superior to SGLT2i, which often show more pronounced effects on preventing heart failure progression and kidney failure. <cite id="35208256">Few real‑world studies on renal outcomes suggest SGLT2i and GLP‑1 RA each reduce eGFR decline and hard renal events, but GLP‑1 RA was less effective than SGLT2i on heart failure prevention; GLP‑1 RA’s renal benefit was not evident versus SGLT2i</cite>.

# Safety and adverse events

Safety profiles differ between classes and complement their efficacy. SGLT2i increase genital infections with high certainty, while GLP‑1 RA may increase severe gastrointestinal events with lower certainty. <cite id="33441402">SGLT2i cause genital infection (high certainty), whereas GLP‑1 RA might cause severe gastrointestinal events (low certainty); both classes reduce mortality, myocardial infarction, and kidney failure</cite>. In meta‑analysis restricted to patients with diabetes, SGLT2i reduced serious adverse events relative to placebo irrespective of background GLP‑1 RA use, supporting overall net benefit. <cite id="38991584">Across 12 trials, SGLT2i reduced serious adverse events versus placebo regardless of whether patients were on GLP‑1 RA</cite>.

# Combination therapy and additivity

Evidence supports independent mechanisms and additive benefits when SGLT2i and GLP‑1 RA are used together. In a large collaborative meta‑analysis, SGLT2i reduced MACE and improved CKD progression even in patients receiving GLP‑1 RA, and GLP‑1 RA efficacy was unaffected by SGLT2i background. <cite id="38991584">SGLT2i effects on MACE, heart failure or cardiovascular death, CKD progression, and eGFR slope were consistent regardless of GLP‑1 RA use; fewer serious adverse events occurred with SGLT2i vs placebo irrespective of GLP‑1 RA</cite>. Post‑hoc and pooled analyses of GLP‑1 RA trials similarly found no interaction with SGLT2i background, suggesting combination therapy can further lower CV risk. <cite id="37532422">GLP‑1 RA reduced MACE and heart failure hospitalization independently of SGLT2i background, supporting additivity</cite>.

# Practical implications for patients with established ASCVD

- Both SGLT2i and GLP‑1 RA reduce major atherosclerotic events in established ASCVD, with no clear overall superiority on composite MACE; however, GLP‑1 RA shows a relative advantage for reducing stroke, while SGLT2i more consistently prevent heart failure hospitalization and slow CKD progression. <cite id="34536085">No difference in 3P‑MACE between SGLT2i and GLP‑1 RA; GLP‑1 RA lowers stroke risk, SGLT2i lower HHF and renal outcomes</cite> <cite id="32797182">Both reduce 3P‑MACE in ASCVD subgroups</cite> <cite id="36335326">SGLT2i show stronger renal and HHF effects than GLP‑1 RA in T2D with CKD</cite> <cite id="35208256">Real‑world analyses show similar composite CV effects across classes but SGLT2i better at preventing heart failure</cite>.
- In patients with high ASCVD burden or significant comorbidity (HF, CKD), SGLT2i may be preferred due to stronger renal protection and heart failure risk reduction; in patients prioritizing atherosclerotic event reduction or with contraindications to SGLT2i (e.g., genital infection risk), GLP‑1 RA remains effective and independent. <cite id="34536085">SGLT2i superiority for HHF and renal outcomes supports selection in HF/CKD comorbid ASCVD</cite> <cite id="37532422">GLP‑1 RA efficacy independent of SGLT2i background supports flexible selection</cite>.
- Combination therapy is increasingly supported by trial evidence and meta‑analyses, potentially offering additive CV and renal protection; individualized risk stratification (e.g., phenotyping) can guide which patients derive the greatest benefit from which agent or combination. <cite id="38991584">Consistent benefits of SGLT2i regardless of GLP‑1 RA and vice versa support independent mechanisms and combination use</cite> <cite id="39301712">Phenotype‑driven risk stratification shows large heterogeneity in ASCVD benefit from canagliflozin</cite> <cite id="35120199">Machine‑learning phenotyping identifies patients with greater ASCVD benefit from canagliflozin and validates this in a renal cohort</cite>.

# Limitations and evidence gaps

- Direct head‑to‑head agent‑level trials comparing SGLT2i vs GLP‑1 RA in pure ASCVD populations are limited; most evidence is indirect via network meta‑analysis and trial subgroup analyses. <cite id="34536085">No direct SGLT2i vs GLP‑1 RA superiority on 3P‑MACE in pooled analysis</cite>.
- Some renal outcome data come from T2D with CKD populations rather than isolated ASCVD cohorts; nonetheless, they inform comparative renal protection. <cite id="36335326">T2D with CKD meta‑analysis shows SGLT2i renal superiority</cite> <cite id="35208256">Real‑world renal outcomes suggest GLP‑1 RA not superior to SGLT2i for kidney protection</cite>.
- Safety trade‑offs (e.g., genital infections with SGLT2i; gastrointestinal effects with GLP‑1 RA) should be weighed against cardiovascular and renal benefits in individualized decision‑making. <cite id="33441402">Documented differences in adverse events support individualized selection</cite>.

# Summary

Among patients with established ASCVD in large outcome trials, SGLT2i and GLP‑1 RA each reduce major atherosclerotic events, with complementary strengths: GLP‑1 RA shows relative benefit for stroke reduction and consistent atherosclerotic event reduction, while SGLT2i more strongly reduce heart failure hospitalization and slow renal decline. These effects are largely independent and additive when combined, and both classes are safe with clear risk‑benefit profiles. Selection should be individualized by ASCVD phenotype, comorbid HF/CKD, patient preferences, and contraindications, with combination therapy considered to maximize CV and renal protection. <cite id="34536085">SGLT2i and GLP‑1 RA reduce 3P‑MACE; SGLT2i better for HHF and renal outcomes; GLP‑1 RA better for stroke</cite> <cite id="32797182">Both classes benefit ASCVD subgroups</cite> <cite id="38991584">Consistent benefits irrespective of the other class and fewer serious adverse events with SGLT2i</cite> <cite id="37532422">GLP‑1 RA efficacy independent of SGLT2i background</cite> <cite id="36335326">SGLT2i show stronger renal and HHF effects than GLP‑1 RA in T2D with CKD</cite> <cite id="35208256">Real‑world evidence supports class‑specific strengths and complementarity</cite> <cite id="39301712">Phenotypic heterogeneity in ASCVD risk and benefit from SGLT2i</cite> <cite id="35120199">Predictable ASCVD benefit heterogeneity across patients and validation in renal cohorts</cite>.

<snippet id="24494633">Title: Impact of diagnosis and early treatment on the course of multiple sclerosis.
Authors: Noyes, Katia, Weinstock-Guttman, Bianca | Year: 2013 | Journal: The American journal of managed care
Abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a progressive inflammatory disease of the central nervous system that results in neurological dysfunction and disability. The initiation of disease-modifying therapy (DMT) early in the course of MS may improve the prognosis for patients with MS and reduce the occurrence of neurological damage. In patients with relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS), DMT reduces the rate of relapses, reduces the appearance of magnetic resonance imaging markers of disease activity, and slows the course of disability progression. DMT has been shown to be more effective when initiated early in the course of MS. In patients who have not yet developed clinically definite MS (CDMS), but have had 1 attack of neurological symptoms consistent with MS (ie, clinically isolated syndrome [CIS]), the initiation of DMT (specifically, interferon beta, glatiramer acetate, and teriflunomide) following this attack has been shown to delay the conversion to CDMS. Current guidelines have recognized the benefits of early treatment of MS with DMTs. However, there are a number of barriers to implementing early MS treatment. Early diagnosis and treatment of MS can be hindered because patients may delay consulting a physician about their neurological symptoms or may be reluctant to start DMT. Further, even after initiating DMT, continued adherence to treatment is often poor. These delays in treatment and a lack of adherence to treatment are associated with poor patient outcomes. The objectives of this review are to highlight the importance of early diagnosis and treatment of CIS or RRMS and discuss the favorable outcomes associated with early initiation of DMT.</snippet>
<snippet id="38730097">Title: Long-term clinical outcomes in patients with CIS treated with interferon beta-1b: results from the 15-year follow up of the BENEFIT trial.
Authors: Kappos, Ludwig, Edan, Gilles, Freedman, Mark S et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Journal of neurology
Abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) treatment intervention with immunomodulating therapy at early disease stage improves short term clinical outcomes. The objective of this study is to describe the long-term outcomes and healthcare utilization of patients with clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) included in the Betaferon®/Betaseron® in Newly Emerging MS for Initial Treatment (BENEFIT) randomized, parallel group trial. In BENEFIT patients were assigned to "early" IFNB-1b treatment or placebo ("delayed" treatment). After 2 years or conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS), all patients were offered IFNB-1b and were reassessed 15 years later. Of 468 patients, 261 (55.8%) were enrolled into BENEFIT 15 (161 [55.1%] from the early, 100 [56.8%] from the delayed treatment arm). In the full BENEFIT analysis set, risk of conversion to CDMS remained lower in the early treatment group ( - 30.5%; hazard ratio 0.695 [95% CI, 0.547-0.883]; p = 0.0029) with a 15.7% lower risk of relapse than in the delayed treatment group (p = 0.1008). Overall, 25 patients (9.6%; 9.9% early, 9.0% delayed) converted to secondary progressive multiple sclerosis. Disability remained low and stable with no significant difference between groups in Expanded Disability Status Scale score or MRI metrics. Paced Auditory Serial Addition Task-3 scores were better in the early treatment group (p = 0.0036 for treatment effect over 15 years). 66.3% of patients were still employed at Year 15 versus 74.7% at baseline. In conclusion, results 15 years from initial randomization support long-term benefits of early treatment with IFNB-1b.</snippet>
<snippet id="22206762">Title: Early treatment in multiple sclerosis.
Authors: Elovaara, Irina | Year: 2011 | Journal: Journal of the neurological sciences
Abstract: There is now a consensus that early treatment of patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis is desirable, mainly because early treatment may delay the accumulation of disability, but also because disease-modifying treatments seem to be more effective when started early in the course of the disease. In particular, all current first-line disease-modifying treatments have also been shown to be effective in treating clinically isolated syndrome. The evidence for this comes from extensive experience in randomised controlled Phase III clinical trials. While many patients presenting a clinically isolated syndrome are at high risk of experiencing a second attack, early treatment with all disease-modifying treatments has been shown to delay conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis when compared to late treatment. Some of these trials have completed five years of follow-up. While the evidence for early intervention is stronger than ever, it is worthwhile to consider its relevance to everyday clinical practice. In particular, it is important to determine which patients are the best candidates for early therapy and to evaluate the anticipated risks and benefits of choosing a given therapy for a given patient.</snippet>
<snippet id="23234810">Title: Effects of early treatment with glatiramer acetate in patients with clinically isolated syndrome.
Authors: Comi, Giancarlo, Martinelli, Vittorio, Rodegher, Mariaemma et al. | Year: 2013 | Journal: Multiple sclerosis (Houndmills, Basingstoke, England)
Abstract: BACKGROUND
The placebo-controlled phase of the PreCISe study showed that glatiramer acetate delayed onset of clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS) in patients with clinically isolated syndrome and brain lesions on MRI.
OBJECTIVE
To compare the effects of early versus delayed glatiramer acetate treatment in the open-label phase of PreCISe.
METHODS
Patients with a clinically isolated syndrome suggestive of MS with unifocal manifestation and ≥2 T2-weighted brain lesions were randomized to receive glatiramer acetate 20 mg/d (early-treatment, n=198) or placebo (delayed-treatment, n=211) for 36 months or until conversion to CDMS, followed by open-label glatiramer acetate treatment for two years.
RESULTS
Early glatiramer acetate treatment reduced CDMS conversion risk by 41% (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% confidence interval 0.44-0.80; p=0.0005) versus delayed-treatment, and was associated with a 972-day delay (185%) in conversion to CDMS, less brain atrophy (-28%, p=0.0209), fewer new T2 lesions/year (-42%, <0.0001) and lower T2 lesion volume (-22%, p=0.0005) versus delayed treatment. Adverse events were consistent with the established safety profile of glatiramer acetate.
CONCLUSIONS
Effects of early glatiramer acetate treatment on the rate of conversion to CDMS and on MRI measures of disease activity and lesion burden support initiating glatiramer acetate treatment soon after the first clinical symptoms suggestive of MS and continuing treatment to sustain benefits.</snippet>
<snippet id="19901165">Title: Magnetic resonance imaging predictors of conversion to multiple sclerosis in the BENEFIT study.
Authors: Moraal, Bastiaan, Pohl, Christoph, Uitdehaag, Bernard M J et al. | Year: 2009 | Journal: Archives of neurology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Several studies have confirmed the predictive value of baseline and follow-up magnetic resonance (MR) imaging variables for conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS), depending on the population, follow-up duration, and treatment intervention. However, the timing of follow-up imaging and the effect of treatment intervention on the predictive value of baseline MR imaging variables require further elucidation.
OBJECTIVES
To assess the prognostic value of baseline MR imaging variables for conversion to CDMS over 3 years and whether this was affected by treatment intervention and (2) to assess the increased risk for conversion posed by dissemination in time on follow-up MR imaging.
DESIGN
Cohort study.
SETTING
Multicenter randomized clinical trial.
PATIENTS
Four hundred sixty-eight patients with a clinically isolated syndrome who had an initial clinical demyelinating event within the past 60 days who received early treatment (3 years of interferon beta-1b) or delayed treatment (placebo first, followed by > or =1 year of interferon beta-1b). Intervention Magnetic resonance imaging. Main Outcome Measure Time to CDMS.
RESULTS
The overall conversion rate to CDMS was 42%. Barkhof criteria with the strongest prognostic value were the presence at baseline of at least 9 T2-weighted lesions (hazard ratio [HR], 1.64; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.15-2.33; P = .006) and at least 3 periventricular lesions (1.66; 1.14-2.41; P = .009). No specific advantage was noted in using a fixed cutoff of at least 3 Barkhof criteria (HR, 1.31; 95% CI, 0.95-1.79; P = .10). The prognostic value of all MR imaging criteria was unaffected by treatment intervention (P > or = .20 for all). Dissemination in time resulted in increased risk for CDMS only in patients without dissemination in space at baseline and was most informative at the 9-month MR imaging (HR, 2.72; 95% CI, 1.26-5.87; P = .01).
CONCLUSIONS
The modified Barkhof criteria showed moderate predictive value for conversion to CDMS, although all patients had received interferon beta-1b therapy for at least 1 year. The predictive value was unaffected by treatment intervention. Follow-up MR imaging was most informative after 9 months in patients without dissemination in space at baseline.</snippet>

<snippet id="31811811">Title: What do we currently know about the clinically isolated syndrome suggestive of multiple sclerosis? An update.
Authors: Grzegorski, Tomasz, Losy, Jacek | Year: 2020 | Journal: Reviews in the neurosciences
Abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic, demyelinating, not fully understood disease of the central nervous system. The first demyelinating clinical episode is called clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) suggestive of MS. Although the most common manifestations of CIS are long tracts dysfunction and unilateral optic neuritis, it can also include isolated brainstem syndromes, cerebellar involvement, and polysymptomatic clinical image. Recently, the frequency of CIS diagnosis has decreased due to the more sensitive and less specific 2017 McDonald criteria compared with the revisions from 2010. Not all patients with CIS develop MS. The risk of conversion can be estimated based on many predictive factors including epidemiological, ethnical, clinical, biochemical, radiological, immunogenetic, and other markers. The management of CIS is nowadays widely discussed among clinicians and neuroscientists. To date, interferons, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide, cladribine, and some other agents have been evaluated in randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind studies relying on large groups of patients with the first demyelinating event. All of these drugs were shown to have beneficial effects in patients with CIS and might be used routinely in the future. The goal of this article is to explore the most relevant topics regarding CIS as well as to provide the most recent information in the field. The review presents CIS definition, classification, clinical image, predictive factors, and management. What is more, this is one of very few reviews summarizing the topic in the light of the 2017 McDonald criteria.</snippet>
<snippet id="31195337">Title: Long-term outcomes with teriflunomide in patients with clinically isolated syndrome: Results of the TOPIC extension study ★★ .
Authors: Miller, Aaron E, Vermersch, Patrick, Kappos, Ludwig et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: Multiple sclerosis and related disorders
Abstract: BACKGROUND
In the phase 3 TOPIC study, teriflunomide significantly reduced the risk of relapse determining conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS) in patients with clinically isolated syndrome, versus placebo. We assessed clinical and safety outcomes associated with extended teriflunomide treatment in the TOPIC extension study.
METHODS
Patients who completed the TOPIC core study (including those still on study at early termination) or converted to CDMS after at least 24 weeks in the core study were eligible to participate in the extension. The primary efficacy endpoint in the extension was time to conversion to CDMS.
RESULTS
Risk of relapse determining conversion to CDMS was 47.1% lower in patients treated with teriflunomide 14 mg during the core and extension studies compared with patients treated with placebo during the core study and teriflunomide 14 mg during the extension. The incidence of adverse events was 75.8% and 81.9% for 7 and 14 mg teriflunomide, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS
Reduced risk of relapse determining conversion to CDMS in patients with early MS receiving teriflunomide 14 mg in the core study remained throughout the extension supporting the benefits of early treatment. No new safety signals were observed for teriflunomide 7 or 14 mg.</snippet>

<snippet id="25192851">Title: Oral teriflunomide for patients with a first clinical episode suggestive of multiple sclerosis (TOPIC): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial.
Authors: Miller, Aaron E, Wolinsky, Jerry S, Kappos, Ludwig et al. | Year: 2014 | Journal: The Lancet. Neurology
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Teriflunomide is a once-daily oral immunomodulator approved for the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. We aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of teriflunomide in patients with a first clinical episode suggestive of multiple sclerosis.
METHODS
In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study, we enrolled patients aged 18-55 years with clinically isolated syndrome (defined as a neurological event consistent with demyelination, starting within 90 days of randomisation, and two or more T2-weighted MRI lesions ≥3 mm in diameter) from 112 centres (mostly hospitals) in 20 countries. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1) in a double-blind manner (by an interactive voice response system) to once-daily oral teriflunomide 14 mg, teriflunomide 7 mg, or placebo, for up to 108 weeks. Patients, staff administering the interventions, and outcome assessors were masked to treatment assignment. The primary endpoint was time to relapse (a new neurological abnormality separated by ≥30 days from a preceding clinical event, present for ≥24 h in the absence of fever or known infection), which defined conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis. The key secondary endpoint was time to relapse or new gadolinium-enhancing or T2 lesions on MRI, whichever occurred first. The primary outcome was analysed for the modified intention-to-treat population; safety analyses included all randomised patients who were exposed to the study drug, as treated. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, number NCT00622700.
FINDINGS
Between Feb 13, 2008, and Aug 22, 2012, 618 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to teriflunomide 14 mg (n=216), teriflunomide 7 mg (n=205), or placebo (n=197). Two patients in each of the teriflunomide groups did not receive the study drug, so the modified intention-to-treat population comprised 214 patients in the teriflunomide 14 mg group, 203 in the teriflunomide 7 mg group, and 197 in the placebo group. Compared with placebo, teriflunomide significantly reduced the risk of relapse defining clinically definite multiple sclerosis at the 14 mg dose (hazard ratio [HR] 0·574 [95% CI 0·379-0·869]; p=0·0087) and at the 7 mg dose (0·628 [0·416-0·949]; p=0·0271). TOPIC is to our knowledge the first study to report benefits of an available oral disease-modifying therapy in patients with early multiple sclerosis. These results extend the stages of multiple sclerosis in which teriflunomide shows a beneficial effect.

# Bottom line

Early initiation of disease‑modifying therapy (DMT) in clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) reduces the risk of conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS) compared with delayed treatment, across multiple randomized trials and long‑term follow‑ups. The relative risk reduction is substantial for several agents, and benefits are seen even when treatment is started after a single demyelinating event.

# Evidence from randomized trials and long‑term data

- Interferon beta‑1b (IFNβ‑1b): In the BENEFIT trial, early IFNβ‑1b versus delayed treatment showed a significantly lower conversion to CDMS at 2 years (hazard ratio 0.695, 95% CI 0.547–0.883; p=0.0029; absolute risk difference −30.5%), with sustained long‑term benefits up to 15 years, including lower relapse risk and preserved function in the early‑treated group. <cite id="38730097">In BENEFIT patients were assigned to "early" IFNB-1b treatment or placebo ("delayed" treatment). # Reviews and consensus

Reviews conclude that early treatment of CIS—after a single demyelinating event—is beneficial and that multiple DMTs (interferons, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide, cladribine) have demonstrated efficacy in delaying conversion to CDMS. <cite id="24494633">In patients who have not yet developed clinically definite MS but have had one attack consistent with MS (CIS), initiation of DMT (interferon beta, glatiramer acetate, and teriflunomide) following this attack has been shown to delay the conversion to CDMS.</cite> <cite id="22206762">All current first-line disease-modifying treatments have also been shown to be effective in treating clinically isolated syndrome... early treatment with all disease-modifying treatments has been shown to delay conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis when compared to late treatment.</cite> <cite id="31811811">Interferons, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide, cladribine, and some other agents have been evaluated in randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind studies in patients with the first demyelinating event... Across agents and trial designs, initiating DMT soon after CIS is associated with a lower hazard of conversion to CDMS and improved downstream outcomes (fewer relapses, less MRI activity/lesion burden, and better long‑term function and independence). data.title: Impact of diagnosis and early treatment on the course of multiple sclerosis.
data.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a progressive inflammatory disease of the central nervous system that results in neurological dysfunction and disability. The initiation of disease-modifying therapy (DMT) early in the course of MS may improve the prognosis for patients with MS and reduce the occurrence of neurological damage. In patients with relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS), DMT reduces the rate of relapses, reduces the appearance of magnetic resonance imaging markers of disease activity, and slows the course of disability progression. DMT has been shown to be more effective when initiated early in the course of MS. In patients who have not yet developed clinically definite MS (CDMS), but have had 1 attack of neurological symptoms consistent with MS (ie, clinically isolated syndrome [CIS]), the initiation of DMT (specifically, interferon beta, glatiramer acetate, and teriflunomide) following this attack has been shown to delay the conversion to CDMS. Current guidelines have recognized the benefits of early treatment of MS with DMTs. However, there are a number of barriers to implementing early MS treatment. Early diagnosis and treatment of MS can be hindered because patients may delay consulting a physician about their neurological symptoms or may be reluctant to start DMT. Further, even after initiating DMT, continued adherence to treatment is often poor. These delays in treatment and a lack of adherence to treatment are associated with poor patient outcomes. The objectives of this review are to highlight the importance of early diagnosis and treatment of CIS or RRMS and discuss the favorable outcomes associated with early initiation of DMT.

data.title: Long-term clinical outcomes in patients with CIS treated with interferon beta-1b: results from the 15-year follow up of the BENEFIT trial.
data.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) treatment intervention with immunomodulating therapy at early disease stage improves short term clinical outcomes. The objective of this study is to describe the long-term outcomes and healthcare utilization of patients with clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) included in the Betaferon®/Betaseron® in Newly Emerging MS for Initial Treatment (BENEFIT) randomized, parallel group trial. In BENEFIT patients were assigned to "early" IFNB-1b treatment or placebo ("delayed" treatment). After 2 years or conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS), all patients were offered IFNB-1b and were reassessed 15 years later. Of 468 patients, 261 (55.8%) were enrolled into BENEFIT 15 (161 [55.1%] from the early, 100 [56.8%] from the delayed treatment arm). In the full BENEFIT analysis set, risk of conversion to CDMS remained lower in the early treatment group ( - 30.5%; hazard ratio 0.695 [95% CI, 0.547-0.883]; p = 0.0029) with a 15.7% lower risk of relapse than in the delayed treatment group (p = 0.1008). Overall, 25 patients (9.6%; 9.9% early, 9.0% delayed) converted to secondary progressive multiple sclerosis. Disability remained low and stable with no significant difference between groups in Expanded Disability Status Scale score or MRI metrics. Paced Auditory Serial Addition Task-3 scores were better in the early treatment group (p = 0.0036 for treatment effect over 15 years). 66.3% of patients were still employed at Year 15 versus 74.7% at baseline. In conclusion, results 15 years from initial randomization support long-term benefits of early treatment with IFNB-1b.

data.title: Early treatment in multiple sclerosis.
data.abstract: There is now a consensus that early treatment of patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis is desirable, mainly because early treatment may delay the accumulation of disability, but also because disease-modifying treatments seem to be more effective when started early in the course of the disease. In particular, all current first-line disease-modifying treatments have also been shown to be effective in treating clinically isolated syndrome. The evidence for this comes from extensive experience in randomised controlled Phase III clinical trials. While many patients presenting a clinically isolated syndrome are at high risk of experiencing a second attack, early treatment with all disease-modifying treatments has been shown to delay conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis when compared to late treatment. Some of these trials have completed five years of follow-up. While the evidence for early intervention is stronger than ever, it is worthwhile to consider its relevance to everyday clinical practice. In particular, it is important to determine which patients are the best candidates for early therapy and to evaluate the anticipated risks and benefits of choosing a given therapy for a given patient.

data.title: Effects of early treatment with glatiramer acetate in patients with clinically isolated syndrome.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
The placebo-controlled phase of the PreCISe study showed that glatiramer acetate delayed onset of clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS) in patients with clinically isolated syndrome and brain lesions on MRI.
OBJECTIVE
To compare the effects of early versus delayed glatiramer acetate treatment in the open-label phase of PreCISe.
METHODS
Patients with a clinically isolated syndrome suggestive of MS with unifocal manifestation and ≥2 T2-weighted brain lesions were randomized to receive glatiramer acetate 20 mg/d (early-treatment, n=198) or placebo (delayed-treatment, n=211) for 36 months or until conversion to CDMS, followed by open-label glatiramer acetate treatment for two years.
RESULTS
Early glatiramer acetate treatment reduced CDMS conversion risk by 41% (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% confidence interval 0.44-0.80; p=0.0005) versus delayed-treatment, and was associated with a 972-day delay (185%) in conversion to CDMS, less brain atrophy (-28%, p=0.0209), fewer new T2 lesions/year (-42%, <0.0001) and lower T2 lesion volume (-22%, p=0.0005) versus delayed treatment. Adverse events were consistent with the established safety profile of glatiramer acetate.
CONCLUSIONS
Effects of early glatiramer acetate treatment on the rate of conversion to CDMS and on MRI measures of disease activity and lesion burden support initiating glatiramer acetate treatment soon after the first clinical symptoms suggestive of MS and continuing treatment to sustain benefits.

data.title: Magnetic resonance imaging predictors of conversion to multiple sclerosis in the BENEFIT study.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Several studies have confirmed the predictive value of baseline and follow-up magnetic resonance (MR) imaging variables for conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS), depending on the population, follow-up duration, and treatment intervention. However, the timing of follow-up imaging and the effect of treatment intervention on the predictive value of baseline MR imaging variables require further elucidation.
OBJECTIVES
To assess the prognostic value of baseline MR imaging variables for conversion to CDMS over 3 years and whether this was affected by treatment intervention and (2) to assess the increased risk for conversion posed by dissemination in time on follow-up MR imaging.
DESIGN
Cohort study.
SETTING
Multicenter randomized clinical trial.
PATIENTS
Four hundred sixty-eight patients with a clinically isolated syndrome who had an initial clinical demyelinating event within the past 60 days who received early treatment (3 years of interferon beta-1b) or delayed treatment (placebo first, followed by > or =1 year of interferon beta-1b). Intervention Magnetic resonance imaging. Main Outcome Measure Time to CDMS.
RESULTS
The overall conversion rate to CDMS was 42%. Barkhof criteria with the strongest prognostic value were the presence at baseline of at least 9 T2-weighted lesions (hazard ratio [HR], 1.64; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.15-2.33; P = .006) and at least 3 periventricular lesions (1.66; 1.14-2.41; P = .009). No specific advantage was noted in using a fixed cutoff of at least 3 Barkhof criteria (HR, 1.31; 95% CI, 0.95-1.79; P = .10). The prognostic value of all MR imaging criteria was unaffected by treatment intervention (P > or = .20 for all). Dissemination in time resulted in increased risk for CDMS only in patients without dissemination in space at baseline and was most informative at the 9-month MR imaging (HR, 2.72; 95% CI, 1.26-5.87; P = .01).
CONCLUSIONS
The modified Barkhof criteria showed moderate predictive value for conversion to CDMS, although all patients had received interferon beta-1b therapy for at least 1 year. The predictive value was unaffected by treatment intervention. Follow-up MR imaging was most informative after 9 months in patients without dissemination in space at baseline.

data.title: Long-term outcomes with teriflunomide in patients with clinically isolated syndrome: Results of the TOPIC extension study ★★ .
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
In the phase 3 TOPIC study, teriflunomide significantly reduced the risk of relapse determining conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS) in patients with clinically isolated syndrome, versus placebo. We assessed clinical and safety outcomes associated with extended teriflunomide treatment in the TOPIC extension study.
METHODS
Patients who completed the TOPIC core study (including those still on study at early termination) or converted to CDMS after at least 24 weeks in the core study were eligible to participate in the extension. The primary efficacy endpoint in the extension was time to conversion to CDMS.
RESULTS
Risk of relapse determining conversion to CDMS was 47.1% lower in patients treated with teriflunomide 14 mg during the core and extension studies compared with patients treated with placebo during the core study and teriflunomide 14 mg during the extension. The incidence of adverse events was 75.8% and 81.9% for 7 and 14 mg teriflunomide, respectively.
CONCLUSIONS
Reduced risk of relapse determining conversion to CDMS in patients with early MS receiving teriflunomide 14 mg in the core study remained throughout the extension supporting the benefits of early treatment. No new safety signals were observed for teriflunomide 7 or 14 mg.

data.title: Oral teriflunomide for patients with a first clinical episode suggestive of multiple sclerosis (TOPIC): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Teriflunomide is a once-daily oral immunomodulator approved for the treatment of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis. We aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of teriflunomide in patients with a first clinical episode suggestive of multiple sclerosis.
METHODS
In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study, we enrolled patients aged 18-55 years with clinically isolated syndrome (defined as a neurological event consistent with demyelination, starting within 90 days of randomisation, and two or more T2-weighted MRI lesions ≥3 mm in diameter) from 112 centres (mostly hospitals) in 20 countries. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1) in a double-blind manner (by an interactive voice response system) to once-daily oral teriflunomide 14 mg, teriflunomide 7 mg, or placebo, for up to 108 weeks. Patients, staff administering the interventions, and outcome assessors were masked to treatment assignment. The primary endpoint was time to relapse (a new neurological abnormality separated by ≥30 days from a preceding clinical event, present for ≥24 h in the absence of fever or known infection), which defined conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis. The key secondary endpoint was time to relapse or new gadolinium-enhancing or T2 lesions on MRI, whichever occurred first. The primary outcome was analysed for the modified intention-to-treat population; safety analyses included all randomised patients who were exposed to the study drug, as treated. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, number NCT00622700.
FINDINGS
Between Feb 13, 2008, and Aug 22, 2012, 618 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to teriflunomide 14 mg (n=216), teriflunomide 7 mg (n=205), or placebo (n=197). Two patients in each of the teriflunomide groups did not receive the study drug, so the modified intention-to-treat population comprised 214 patients in the teriflunomide 14 mg group, 203 in the teriflunomide 7 mg group, and 197 in the placebo group. Compared with placebo, teriflunomide significantly reduced the risk of relapse defining clinically definite multiple sclerosis at the 14 mg dose (hazard ratio [HR] 0·574 [95% CI 0·379-0·869]; p=0·0087) and at the 7 mg dose (0·628 [0·416-0·949]; p=0·0271). Teriflunomide reduced the risk of relapse or a new MRI lesion compared with placebo at the 14 mg dose (HR 0·651 [95% CI 0·515-0·822]; p=0·0003) and at the 7 mg dose (0·686 [0·540-0·871]; p=0·0020). During the study, six patients who were randomly assigned to placebo accidently also received teriflunomide at some point: four received 7 mg and two received 14 mg. Therefore, the safety population comprised 216 patients on teriflunomide 14 mg, 207 on teriflunomide 7 mg, and 191 on placebo. Adverse events that occurred in at least 10% of patients in either teriflunomide group and with an incidence that was at least 2% higher than that with placebo were increased alanine aminotransferase (40 [19%] of 216 patients in the 14 mg group, 36 [17%] of 207 in the 7 mg group vs 27 [14%] of 191 in the placebo group), hair thinning (25 [12%] and 12 [6%] vs 15 [8%]), diarrhoea (23 [11%] and 28 [14%] vs 12 [6%]), paraesthesia (22 [10%] and 11 [5%] vs 10 [5%]), and upper respiratory tract infection (20 [9%] and 23 [11%] vs 14 [7%]). The most common serious adverse event was an increase in alanine aminotransferase (four [2%] and five [2%] vs three [2%]).
INTERPRETATION
TOPIC is to our knowledge the first study to report benefits of an available oral disease-modifying therapy in patients with early multiple sclerosis. These results extend the stages of multiple sclerosis in which teriflunomide shows a beneficial effect.

data.title: Long-term follow-up of patients with a first clinical demyelinating event (clinically isolated syndrome) who received cladribine tablets in CLASSIC-MS: Findings for the ORACLE-MS cohort.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
CLASSIC-MS explored long-term outcomes of patients treated with cladribine tablets.
OBJECTIVE
Assess long-term efficacy in patients previously enrolled in ORACLE-MS, a Phase III parent trial.
METHODS
ORACLE-MS included patients with a first clinical demyelinating event (FCDE or clinically isolated syndrome) who received ⩾1 course of cladribine tablets or placebo. With a median follow-up time of 9.5 years, CLASSIC-MS assessed conversion rates to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS), time-to-conversion, relapse rates, long-term mobility/disability status and subsequent disease-modifying therapy (DMT) use.
RESULTS
Of 227 patients from the ORACLE-MS cohort of 616, 68.7% were exposed to cladribine tablets and 31.3% were never exposed. Of the exposed patients at risk, 51.5% converted to CDMS with a median conversion time of 8.4 (95% confidence interval (CI): 5.4-not estimable) years, versus 80.6%, median time 0.8 (95% CI: 0.3-2.4) years, for never exposed. Exposed patients were less likely to be using a wheelchair or ambulatory device or receive subsequent DMTs, and 53.2% were relapse-free versus 28.2% never exposed.
CONCLUSIONS
Proportionally, more FCDE patients exposed to cladribine tablets experienced delayed conversion to CDMS and fewer relapses and were less likely to use a wheelchair or ambulatory device than never-exposed patients, at 9.5 years (median).

data.title: What do we currently know about the clinically isolated syndrome suggestive of multiple sclerosis? An update.
data.abstract: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic, demyelinating, not fully understood disease of the central nervous system. The first demyelinating clinical episode is called clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) suggestive of MS. Although the most common manifestations of CIS are long tracts dysfunction and unilateral optic neuritis, it can also include isolated brainstem syndromes, cerebellar involvement, and polysymptomatic clinical image. Recently, the frequency of CIS diagnosis has decreased due to the more sensitive and less specific 2017 McDonald criteria compared with the revisions from 2010. Not all patients with CIS develop MS. The risk of conversion can be estimated based on many predictive factors including epidemiological, ethnical, clinical, biochemical, radiological, immunogenetic, and other markers. The management of CIS is nowadays widely discussed among clinicians and neuroscientists. To date, interferons, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide, cladribine, and some other agents have been evaluated in randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind studies relying on large groups of patients with the first demyelinating event. All of these drugs were shown to have beneficial effects in patients with CIS and might be used routinely in the future. The goal of this article is to explore the most relevant topics regarding CIS as well as to provide the most recent information in the field. The review presents CIS definition, classification, clinical image, predictive factors, and management. What is more, this is one of very few reviews summarizing the topic in the light of the 2017 McDonald criteria.

# Bottom line

Early initiation of disease‑modifying therapy (DMT) in clinically isolated syndrome (CIS) reduces the risk of conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS) compared with delayed treatment, across multiple randomized trials and long‑term follow‑ups. The relative risk reduction is substantial for several agents, and benefits are seen even when treatment is started after a single demyelinating event.

# Evidence from randomized trials and long‑term data

- Interferon beta‑1b (IFNβ‑1b): In the BENEFIT trial, early IFNβ‑1b versus delayed treatment showed a significantly lower conversion to CDMS at 2 years (hazard ratio 0.695, 95% CI 0.547–0.883; p=0.0029; absolute risk difference −30.5%), with sustained long‑term benefits up to 15 years, including lower relapse risk and preserved function in the early‑treated group. <cite id="38730097">In BENEFIT patients were assigned to "early" IFNB-1b treatment or placebo ("delayed" treatment). After 2 years or conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis (CDMS), all patients were offered IFNB-1b and were reassessed 15 years later... In the full BENEFIT analysis set, risk of conversion to CDMS remained lower in the early treatment group ( - 30.5%; hazard ratio 0.695 [95% CI, 0.547-0.883]; p = 0.0029) with a 15.7% lower risk of relapse than in the delayed treatment group.</cite> <cite id="19901165">The overall conversion rate to CDMS was 42%... The prognostic value of all MR imaging criteria was unaffected by treatment intervention.</cite>

- Glatiramer acetate: In the PreCISe study, early glatiramer acetate reduced CDMS conversion risk by 41% versus delayed treatment (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.44–0.80), and delayed conversion by approximately 185% in terms of days (about 972 days), with additional MRI benefits (fewer new T2 lesions and lower lesion volume) and less brain atrophy. <cite id="23234810">Early glatiramer acetate treatment reduced CDMS conversion risk by 41% (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% confidence interval 0.44-0.80; p=0.0005) versus delayed-treatment, and was associated with a 972-day delay (185%) in conversion to CDMS, less brain atrophy (-28%), fewer new T2 lesions/year (-42%) and lower T2 lesion volume (-22%) versus delayed treatment.</cite>

- Teriflunomide: In the phase 3 TOPIC trial, both 7 mg and 14 mg doses significantly reduced the risk of relapse defining CDMS compared with placebo (hazard ratios 0.628 and 0.574, respectively), and also reduced the risk of relapse or new MRI lesions; benefits persisted in long‑term extension. <cite id="25192851">Compared with placebo, teriflunomide significantly reduced the risk of relapse defining clinically definite multiple sclerosis at the 14 mg dose (hazard ratio 0·574 [95% CI 0·379-0·869]; p=0·0087) and at the 7 mg dose (0·628 [0·416-0·949]; p=0·0271)... Teriflunomide reduced the risk of relapse or a new MRI lesion compared with placebo at both doses.</cite> <cite id="31195337">Risk of relapse determining conversion to CDMS was 47.1% lower in patients treated with teriflunomide 14 mg during the core and extension studies compared with patients treated with placebo during the core study and teriflunomide 14 mg during the extension.</cite>

- Cladribine: In the long‑term CLASSIC‑MS follow‑up of the ORACLE‑MS trial (first clinical demyelinating event/CIS), patients exposed to cladribine had markedly lower conversion to CDMS than those never exposed (51.5% vs 80.6% converted; median conversion times 8.4 vs 0.8 years), with additional advantages in relapse‑free status and reduced need for subsequent DMT and mobility aids. <cite id="39690897">Of 227 patients from the ORACLE-MS cohort... 51.5% converted to CDMS with a median conversion time of 8.4 years, versus 80.6% and median 0.8 years for never exposed... Exposed patients were less likely to be using a wheelchair or ambulatory device or receive subsequent DMTs, and 53.2% were relapse-free versus 28.2% never exposed.</cite>

# Reviews and consensus

Reviews conclude that early treatment of CIS—after a single demyelinating event—is beneficial and that multiple DMTs (interferons, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide, cladribine) have demonstrated efficacy in delaying conversion to CDMS. <cite id="24494633">In patients who have not yet developed clinically definite MS but have had one attack consistent with MS (CIS), initiation of DMT (interferon beta, glatiramer acetate, and teriflunomide) following this attack has been shown to delay the conversion to CDMS.</cite> <cite id="22206762">All current first-line disease-modifying treatments have also been shown to be effective in treating clinically isolated syndrome... early treatment with all disease-modifying treatments has been shown to delay conversion to clinically definite multiple sclerosis when compared to late treatment.</cite> <cite id="31811811">Interferons, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide, cladribine, and some other agents have been evaluated in randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind studies in patients with the first demyelinating event... All of these drugs were shown to have beneficial effects in patients with CIS.</cite>

# Interpretation

Across agents and trial designs, initiating DMT soon after CIS is associated with a lower hazard of conversion to CDMS and improved downstream outcomes (fewer relapses, less MRI activity/lesion burden, and better long‑term function and independence). These data support guideline recommendations for early treatment in appropriate CIS patients, particularly those at higher risk of progression. <cite id="38730097">Results 15 years from initial randomization support long-term benefits of early treatment with IFNB-1b.</cite> <cite id="23234810">Effects of early glatiramer acetate on conversion and MRI measures support initiating treatment soon after the first clinical symptoms suggestive of MS.</cite> <cite id="25192851">Teriflunomide shows benefits in the early phase of multiple sclerosis.</cite> <cite id="39690897">Proportionally, more FCDE patients exposed to cladribine experienced delayed conversion and fewer relapses with better long-term mobility and lower subsequent DMT use.</cite>

# Caveats

- Predictors of conversion (e.g., lesion burden on MRI) help stratify risk, and treatment effects on MRI‑predicted conversion may vary by baseline risk profile. <cite id="19901165">The predictive value of MRI criteria was unaffected by treatment intervention, highlighting the importance of baseline risk stratification.</cite>
- Patient selection, adherence, and long‑term safety remain critical considerations; benefits depend on sustained therapy. <cite id="24494633">Delays in treatment and lack of adherence are associated with poor patient outcomes, underscoring the importance of early diagnosis and sustained DMT adherence.</cite>

<snippet id="40654861">Title: Complementary modes of resistance to EGFR TKI in lung adenocarcinoma through MAPK activation and cellular plasticity.
Authors: Zatzman, Matthew, Quintanal-Villalonga, Alvaro, Salehi, Sohrab et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
Abstract: EGFR -mutant lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) represents 20% of all non-small cell lung carcinomas, with most patients presenting with incurable metastatic disease. Treatment with mutant-selective EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) results in initial tumor reduction, yet nearly all patients eventually relapse. The mechanisms driving drug resistance are incompletely understood, creating significant barriers to curing metastatic disease. We integrated clinical genomic and single-nuclei RNA (snRNA) sequencing from a cohort of 62 EGFR -mutant LUAD patients treated with the third generation EGFR TKI, osimertinib, and compared treatment-naïve (TN), minimal residual disease (MRD), and progressive disease (PD) tumors. We found that disease progression is associated with a marked decrease in alveolar lineage fidelity, coincident with reduced MAPK signaling and adenocarcinoma identity. PD tumors with sustained MAPK pathway activity, such as those with EGFR or MET amplifications, tended to retain adenocarcinoma identity. In contrast, MAPK-low tumors were more likely to undergo histological transformation to squamous or neuroendocrine lineages. Remarkably, we observed rare tumor cell populations prior to treatment that were poorly differentiated, in some cases with neuroendocrine or squamous features. At progression, these histologically divergent tumor cells increased in prevalence, both in cases with overt histological transformation, and in others with sub-clinical histological plasticity. These findings suggest that pre-existing capacity for histologic plasticity may be a substrate for therapy induced selection. Taken together, our results illuminate genomically encoded MAPK signaling and lineage plasticity as complementary mechanisms of acquired resistance to EGFR TKI in lung adenocarcinoma.</snippet>
<snippet id="32676311">Title: EGFR mutation genotypes affect efficacy and resistance mechanisms of osimertinib in T790M-positive NSCLC patients.
Authors: Zheng, Qiufan, Huang, Yan, Zhao, Hongyun et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Translational lung cancer research
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Osimertinib is a potent third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) with robust activity in advanced EGFR -mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), including those with T790M resistance mutation. However, a broad interpatient variability was observed. This study aimed to evaluate whether EGFR -mutant genotypes affect the clinical outcomes and resistance mechanisms in T790M-positive NSCLC patients receiving osimertinib therapy.
METHODS
All NSCLC patients treated with osimertinib in our institute were screened. We included those with known EGFR -mutant genotypes and T790M positivity. Clinical outcomes including objective response rate (ORR), clinical benefit rate (CBR), progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS), were evaluated and compared between different EGFR genotypes. Patients with next-generation sequencing testing or tumor rebiopsy after osimertinib treatment were analyzed for resistance mechanisms.
RESULTS
ORR, CBR, PFS, and OS were all non-significantly different among patients harboring EGFR exon 19 deletion (19Del, n=136), L858R (n=93), and uncommon mutations (n=6). However, a subset of tumors with deletion starting at E746 (ΔE746, n=98), but not non-ΔE746 tumors (n=38), had better clinical outcomes than L858R tumors (n=93). Frequencies of T790M loss and C797S acquisition after osimertinib treatment were similar between 19Del (n=56) and L858R tumors (n=33). However, compared with L858R tumors (n=33), those with 19Del ΔE746 subtype (n=40) had a higher whereas non-ΔE746 subtype (n=16) had a similar frequency of acquired C797S mutation. Combined analysis of our cohort and public cohort confirmed these findings.
CONCLUSIONS
Our findings indicate that the EGFR 19Del subtypes affect the clinical outcomes and resistance mechanisms to osimertinib in T790M-positive patients. Identifying patients with relatively worse treatment outcomes may be informative for establishing new therapies for these patients.</snippet>
<snippet id="30228210">Title: Landscape of EGFR-Dependent and -Independent Resistance Mechanisms to Osimertinib and Continuation Therapy Beyond Progression in EGFR -Mutant NSCLC.
Authors: Le, Xiuning, Puri, Sonam, Negrao, Marcelo V et al. | Year: 2018 | Journal: Clinical cancer research : an official journal of the American Association for Cancer Research
Abstract: PURPOSE
Osimertinib was initially approved for T790M-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and, more recently, for first-line treatment of EGFR -mutant NSCLC. However, resistance mechanisms to osimertinib have been incompletely described.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN
Using cohorts from The University of Texas MD Anderson Lung Cancer Moonshot GEMINI and Moffitt Cancer Center lung cancer databases, we collected clinical data for patients treated with osimertinib. Molecular profiling analysis was performed at the time of progression in a subset of the patients.
RESULTS
In the 118 patients treated with osimertinib, 42 had molecular profiling at progression. T790M was preserved in 21 (50%) patients and lost in 21 (50%). EGFR C797 and L792 (26%) mutations were the most common resistance mechanism and were observed exclusively in T790M-preserved cases. MET amplification was the second most common alteration (14%). Recurrent alterations were observed in 22 genes/pathways, including PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET. Preclinical studies confirmed MET, PIK3CA, and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition as potential resistance drivers. Alterations of cell-cycle genes were associated with shorter median progression-free survival (PFS, 4.4 vs. 8.8 months, P = 0.01). In 76 patients with progression, osimertinib was continued in 47 cases with a median second PFS (PFS2) of 12.6 months; 21 patients received local consolidation radiation with a median PFS of 15.5 months. Continuation of osimertinib beyond progression was associated with a longer overall survival compared with discontinuation (11.2 vs. 6.1 months, P = 0.02).
CONCLUSIONS
Osimertinib resistance is associated with diverse, predominantly EGFR-independent genomic alterations. Continuation of osimertinib after progression, alone or in conjunction with radiotherapy, may provide prolonged clinical benefit in selected patients. See related commentary by Devarakonda and Govindan, p. 6112 .</snippet>

<snippet id="38357092">Title: Brief Report: Comprehensive Clinicogenomic Profiling of Small Cell Transformation From EGFR -Mutant NSCLC Informs Potential Therapeutic Targets.
Authors: Zhang, Bingnan, Lewis, Whitney, Stewart, C Allison et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: JTO clinical and research reports
Abstract: INTRODUCTION
NSCLC transformation to SCLC has been best characterized with EGFR -mutant NSCLC, with emerging case reports seen in ALK , RET , and KRAS -altered NSCLC. Previous reports revealed transformed SCLC from EGFR -mutant NSCLC portends very poor prognosis and lack effective treatment. Genomic analyses revealed TP53 and RB1 loss of function increase the risk of SCLC transformation. Little has been reported on the detailed clinicogenomic characteristics and potential therapeutic targets for this patient population.
METHODS
In this study, we conducted a single-center retrospective analysis of clinical and genomic characteristics of patients with EGFR -mutant NSCLC transformed to SCLC. Demographic data, treatment course, and clinical molecular testing reports were extracted from electronic medical records. Kaplan-Meier analyses were used to estimate survival outcomes. Next generation sequencing-based assays was used to identify EGFR and co-occurring genetic alterations in tissue or plasma before and after SCLC transformation. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) was performed on a patient-derived-xenograft model generated from a patient with EGFR-NSCLC transformed SCLC tumor.
RESULTS
A total of 34 patients were identified in our study. Median age at initial diagnosis was 58, and median time to SCLC transformation was 24.2 months. 68% were female and 82% were never smokers. 79% of patients were diagnosed as stage IV disease, and over half had brain metastases at baseline. Median overall survival of the entire cohort was 38.3 months from initial diagnoses and 12.4 months from time of SCLC transformation. Most patients harbored EGFR exon19 deletions as opposed to exon21 L858R alteration. Continuing EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor post-transformation did not improve overall survival compared with those patients where tyrosine kinase inhibitor was stopped in our cohort. In the 20 paired pretransformed and post-transformed patient samples, statistically significant enrichment was seen with PIK3CA alterations (p = 0.04) post-transformation. Profiling of longitudinal liquid biopsy samples suggest emergence of SCLC genetic alterations before biopsy-proven SCLC, as shown by increasing variant allele frequency of TP53, RB1, PIK3CA alterations. ScRNA-seq revealed potential therapeutic targets including DLL3, CD276 (B7-H3) and PTK7 were widely expressed in transformed SCLC.
CONCLUSIONS
SCLC transformation is a potential treatment resistance mechanism in driver-mutant NSCLC. In our cohort of 34 EGFR -mutant NSCLC, poor prognosis was observed after SCLC transformation. Clinicogenomic analyses of paired and longitudinal samples identified genomic alterations emerging post-transformation and scRNA-seq reveal potential therapeutic targets in this population. Further studies are needed to rigorously validate biomarkers and therapeutic targets for this patient population.</snippet>

# Summary

In EGFR-mutant NSCLC, acquired resistance to third‑generation EGFR inhibitors (notably osimertinib) most commonly arises through EGFR-dependent mechanisms (T790M re‑emergence and C797S mutation) and a spectrum of EGFR‑independent genomic alterations, with MET amplification, PIK3CA and FGFR pathway alterations, and RET fusions among the most frequent non‑EGFR dependencies. Lineage plasticity and MAPK pathway reactivation also contribute, with histologic transformation (often to squamous or neuroendocrine features) observed in a subset. Reported frequencies vary by cohort and clinical setting, but integrated analyses suggest EGFR‑independent alterations predominate at resistance, and continuation of osimertinib beyond progression can extend survival in selected patients.

# EGFR-Dependent Mechanisms

- T790M re‑emergence and C797S mutation: In a GEMINI/Moffitt cohort (n=118 osimertinib-treated), T790M was preserved in 50% and lost in 50% at progression; EGFR C797/L792 mutations (interpreted as C797S in clinical practice) accounted for 26% of resistance and occurred only in T790M‑preserved cases, indicating a substantial EGFR‑dependent resistance fraction, particularly in T790M‑positive disease. <cite id="30228210">In a GEMINI/Moffitt cohort (n=118 osimertinib-treated), T790M was preserved in 50% and lost in 50% at progression; EGFR C797/L792 mutations accounted for 26% of resistance and occurred only in T790M‑preserved cases</cite>. In a large T790M‑positive cohort, frequencies of T790M loss and C797S acquisition after osimertinib were similar between exon 19 del and L858R tumors, with exon 19 ΔE746 subtypes showing higher acquired C797S frequency than L858R, supporting variability by EGFR genotype. <cite id="32676311">In T790M‑positive patients, frequencies of T790M loss and C797S acquisition after osimertinib were similar between exon 19 del and L858R tumors, and exon 19 ΔE746 subtypes had higher acquired C797S frequency than L858R</cite>.

# EGFR-Independent Mechanisms

- MET amplification: In the GEMINI/Moffitt analysis, MET amplification was the second most common alteration at resistance (14%), and preclinical studies validated MET as a key driver of osimertinib resistance. <cite id="30228210">In the GEMINI/Moffitt analysis, MET amplification was the second most common alteration at resistance (14%), and preclinical studies confirmed MET as a resistance driver</cite>.

- PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET alterations: Recurrent non‑EGFR pathway alterations included PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET, consistent with activation of RTK‑PI3K and related signaling as resistance mechanisms. <cite id="30228210">Recurrent alterations were observed in 22 genes/pathways, including PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET</cite>.

- EMT and lineage plasticity: Integrated single‑nuclei RNA sequencing in an osimertinib‑treated cohort (n=62) showed that MAPK‑low tumors at progression were more likely to undergo histologic transformation to squamous or neuroendocrine lineages, while those maintaining MAPK activity (e.g., with EGFR or MET amplification) tended to retain adenocarcinoma identity; pre‑existing poorly differentiated/neuroendocrine or squamous‑like populations expanded at progression, implicating lineage plasticity as a complementary resistance mechanism. <cite id="40654861">In an osimertinib cohort (n=62), PD tumors with sustained MAPK activity (EGFR or MET amplifications) retained adenocarcinoma identity, whereas MAPK‑low tumors were more likely to transform to squamous or neuroendocrine lineages; pre‑existing poorly differentiated populations expanded at progression, indicating lineage plasticity as a resistance substrate</cite>.

- SCLC transformation: Clinicogenomic profiling of EGFR‑mutant NSCLC patients who transformed to small cell lung cancer (SCLC) identified additional resistance/escape routes; paired and longitudinal analyses showed enrichment for TP53/RB1 loss and PIK3CA alterations post‑transformation, with potential targets such as DLL3, CD276 (B7‑H3), and PTK7 expressed in transformed SCLC. <cite id="38357092">In 34 EGFR‑mutant NSCLC patients who transformed to SCLC, post‑transformation samples showed enrichment for PIK3CA alterations and TP53/RB1 loss; scRNA‑seq highlighted potential targets DLL3, CD276 (B7‑H3), and PTK7</cite>.

# Clinical Frequency and Cohort Observations

data.title: Complementary modes of resistance to EGFR TKI in lung adenocarcinoma through MAPK activation and cellular plasticity.
data.abstract: EGFR -mutant lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) represents 20% of all non-small cell lung carcinomas, with most patients presenting with incurable metastatic disease. Treatment with mutant-selective EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) results in initial tumor reduction, yet nearly all patients eventually relapse. The mechanisms driving drug resistance are incompletely understood, creating significant barriers to curing metastatic disease. We integrated clinical genomic and single-nuclei RNA (snRNA) sequencing from a cohort of 62 EGFR -mutant LUAD patients treated with the third generation EGFR TKI, osimertinib, and compared treatment-naïve (TN), minimal residual disease (MRD), and progressive disease (PD) tumors. We found that disease progression is associated with a marked decrease in alveolar lineage fidelity, coincident with reduced MAPK signaling and adenocarcinoma identity. PD tumors with sustained MAPK pathway activity, such as those with EGFR or MET amplifications, tended to retain adenocarcinoma identity. In contrast, MAPK-low tumors were more likely to undergo histological transformation to squamous or neuroendocrine lineages. Remarkably, we observed rare tumor cell populations prior to treatment that were poorly differentiated, in some cases with neuroendocrine or squamous features. At progression, these histologically divergent tumor cells increased in prevalence, both in cases with overt histological transformation, and in others with sub-clinical histological plasticity. These findings suggest that pre-existing capacity for histologic plasticity may be a substrate for therapy induced selection. Taken together, our results illuminate genomically encoded MAPK signaling and lineage plasticity as complementary mechanisms of acquired resistance to EGFR TKI in lung adenocarcinoma.

data.title: EGFR mutation genotypes affect efficacy and resistance mechanisms of osimertinib in T790M-positive NSCLC patients.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Osimertinib is a potent third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) with robust activity in advanced EGFR -mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), including those with T790M resistance mutation. However, a broad interpatient variability was observed. This study aimed to evaluate whether EGFR -mutant genotypes affect the clinical outcomes and resistance mechanisms in T790M-positive NSCLC patients receiving osimertinib therapy.
METHODS
All NSCLC patients treated with osimertinib in our institute were screened. We included those with known EGFR -mutant genotypes and T790M positivity. Clinical outcomes including objective response rate (ORR), clinical benefit rate (CBR), progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS), were evaluated and compared between different EGFR genotypes. Patients with next-generation sequencing testing or tumor rebiopsy after osimertinib treatment were analyzed for resistance mechanisms.
RESULTS
ORR, CBR, PFS, and OS were all non-significantly different among patients harboring EGFR exon 19 deletion (19Del, n=136), L858R (n=93), and uncommon mutations (n=6). However, a subset of tumors with deletion starting at E746 (ΔE746, n=98), but not non-ΔE746 tumors (n=38), had better clinical outcomes than L858R tumors (n=93). Frequencies of T790M loss and C797S acquisition after osimertinib treatment were similar between 19Del (n=56) and L858R tumors (n=33). However, compared with L858R tumors (n=33), those with 19Del ΔE746 subtype (n=40) had a higher whereas non-ΔE746 subtype (n=16) had a similar frequency of acquired C797S mutation. Combined analysis of our cohort and public cohort confirmed these findings.
CONCLUSIONS
Our findings indicate that the EGFR 19Del subtypes affect the clinical outcomes and resistance mechanisms to osimertinib in T790M-positive patients. Identifying patients with relatively worse treatment outcomes may be informative for establishing new therapies for these patients.

data.title: Landscape of EGFR-Dependent and -Independent Resistance Mechanisms to Osimertinib and Continuation Therapy Beyond Progression in EGFR -Mutant NSCLC.
data.abstract:
PURPOSE
Osimertinib was initially approved for T790M-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and, more recently, for first-line treatment of EGFR -mutant NSCLC. However, resistance mechanisms to osimertinib have been incompletely described.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN
Using cohorts from The University of Texas MD Anderson Lung Cancer Moonshot GEMINI and Moffitt Cancer Center lung cancer databases, we collected clinical data for patients treated with osimertinib. Molecular profiling analysis was performed at the time of progression in a subset of the patients.
RESULTS
In the 118 patients treated with osimertinib, 42 had molecular profiling at progression. T790M was preserved in 21 (50%) patients and lost in 21 (50%). EGFR C797 and L792 (26%) mutations were the most common resistance mechanism and were observed exclusively in T790M-preserved cases. MET amplification was the second most common alteration (14%). Recurrent alterations were observed in 22 genes/pathways, including PIK3CA, FGFR, and RET. Preclinical studies confirmed MET, PIK3CA, and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition as potential resistance drivers. Alterations of cell-cycle genes were associated with shorter median progression-free survival (PFS, 4.4 vs. 8.8 months, P = 0.01). In 76 patients with progression, osimertinib was continued in 47 cases with a median second PFS (PFS2) of 12.6 months; 21 patients received local consolidation radiation with a median PFS of 15.5 months. Continuation of osimertinib beyond progression was associated with a longer overall survival compared with discontinuation (11.2 vs. 6.1 months, P = 0.02).
CONCLUSIONS
Osimertinib resistance is associated with diverse, predominantly EGFR-independent genomic alterations. Continuation of osimertinib after progression, alone or in conjunction with radiotherapy, may provide prolonged clinical benefit in selected patients. See related commentary by Devarakonda and Govindan, p. 6112 .
